text: A top-two run defense undone by the pass defense and, in Week 4, by turnovers. Arizona is 1–3 at −30, 2nd in EPA per rush allowed but 31st against the pass and 25th on defense overall. The offense slid from 13th to 19th in EPA per play after a 36–24 loss at the Giants in which Brissett threw 3 interceptions and the passing game fell to −0.46 EPA per dropback; the defense took the ball away 3 times in the same game.
DVOA still has Arizona 19th (−6.5%). The offense is 12th and special teams 4th, but the defense ranks 29th.

A one-back offense (86% of plays; league 74%) that uses play action on 15% of dropbacks, the fewest in the league, and its two-back looks have cost −0.12 EPA per play. The defense plays the 3rd-fewest defensive backs and blitzes on 23% of dropbacks (8th lowest). Neither rush plan works: +0.31 EPA per dropback with four rushers (league +0.10) and +0.38 with five or more (league 0.00).

Arizona moves before the snap on 60% of plays (11th; league 58%) but is worse when it does: −0.11 EPA per play with motion against +0.09 without, the 8th-largest drop in the league. The defense sees motion more than all but two teams and has held up against it (−0.05 EPA per play). Without motion it is the worst in the league at +0.31, and +0.52 per dropback.

Jacoby Brissett is now 23rd of 33 qualifiers at −0.03 EPA per dropback, with 6 touchdowns and 4 interceptions, 3 of them at New York. He still completes 5.2 points above expectation on short, quick throws (6.3-yard average depth of target and 2.6 seconds to throw, both 3rd lowest). Blitzes are the problem: −0.39 EPA per dropback when opponents send extra rushers against +0.13 when they don't.

Neither back is beating Next Gen Stats' expectation. Jeremiyah Love has 223 yards at 4.1 per carry (−0.09 over expected, 25th of 46 qualifiers) with a 47% success rate, and Tyler Allgeier 3.5 per carry (−0.14) at −0.17 EPA per carry. Backs get 2.1 yards before contact (24th). Arizona has 10 broken tackles (2.5 per game, 15th), 4 of them by Allgeier.

Trey McBride is still the focal point: 31% of the targets, 33 catches for 242 yards and 2 touchdowns, but his EPA per target fell to +0.20 from +0.42 a week ago. Michael Wilson draws 45% of the air yards yet averages 5.9 yards per target at −0.15 EPA. Kendrick Bourne (12 of 14, +0.33 EPA per target) has been the efficient option, while Marvin Harrison Jr. has 5 catches on 13 targets with a 16.4-yard average depth of target and 1.5 yards of separation.

Pass protection is about average: pressure on 22% of dropbacks (14th lowest) and a 4.3% sack rate (8th). Elijah Wilkinson and Hjalte Froholdt have played every snap and Paris Johnson and Isaac Seumalo nearly all of them, with Isaiah Adams and Jon Gaines sharing the fifth spot. The interior run game is the leak: 35 runs up the middle average 2.7 yards at −0.17 EPA, while runs off either end average 5.6 and 7.9 yards.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, a measure that mostly reflects the QB) plus FTN's charting of each sack. For the first time this season FTN put sacks on Brissett: both Week 4 sacks against the Giants were charged to him. The other five were three standard rushes that won and two extended plays. He turns 19% of pressures into sacks (league 26%), so the low sack total is still mostly his quick release.

The run defense is elite (−0.23 EPA per rush, 2nd), but the pass rush is thin by volume at 6.8 pressures per game (25th). It has finished better lately, with 8 sacks and a 6.5% sack rate (12th, up from 24th). Walter Nolen and Josh Sweat have 5 pressures each and a sack apiece, Budda Baker has 1.5 sacks from safety, and four other players have one.

Still the weak spot, 31st in EPA per dropback allowed. Budda Baker has allowed 200 yards and 2 touchdowns on 16 targets (109 passer rating), Denzel Burke 2 touchdowns (101), and Max Melton 137 yards on 17 targets (104); Baker and Burke each have an interception. Andrew Wingard remains the exception, with an interception, a forced fumble, 3 tackles for loss and a 67 rating allowed.

PFR's charting matches the EPA. Arizona has allowed a 106.7 passer rating (30th; league 93.2) and 8.8 yards per target (31st): 69 of 120 for 1,052 yards, 11 touchdowns (30th) and 3 interceptions. Opponents complete only 58% of those throws (6th lowest), but the catches are big ones. Linebackers have fared worst (114.4 rating on 31 targets, 30th among linebacker groups), and the safeties give up 13.4 yards per target.

A strength, 4th in special teams DVOA. Chad Ryland is 8 of 9 on field goals with a 60-yarder and 9 of 9 on extra points. Blake Gillikin has 7 of 20 punts inside the 20, and Jalen Brooks (26.2) and Devin Duvernay (29.5) both average over 26 yards per kickoff return.

Two straight wins since Michael Penix Jr. took over have pulled Atlanta to 2–2 and a +4 point differential. The offense has climbed to 18th in EPA per play (from 29th) and 5th in success rate, and the 45–24 win at New Orleans (+0.42 EPA per play, 422 yards, no turnovers) was its best game yet. The defense is 8th in EPA per play and 1st against the run. Giveaways (8) still outnumber takeaways (3), nearly all of that from Weeks 1 and 2.
DVOA has caught up with the turnaround: Atlanta is 15th overall (from 23rd), with the offense up to 17th (from 27th) and the defense 8th. Special teams are still 27th.

A run-first offense (28th in pass rate over expected) that keeps about 1.6 tight ends on the field, 6th most. Two-back looks make up 25% of plays (league 20%) and have produced +0.28 EPA per play, against −0.14 with one back. The defense rushes four on 76% of dropbacks (league 66%) and blitzes on 23% by FTN's count (26th). Sending five or more has been slightly better so far (−0.04 EPA per dropback against +0.06 with four).

Motion is what makes the passing game work. Atlanta motions on 63% of plays (9th; league 58%), and its gain from motion, +0.23 EPA per play, is 5th largest. Dropbacks with motion are at −0.02 EPA against −0.49 without, the 2nd-biggest passing gap in the league, while runs do as well without it (+0.15) as with it (+0.11). On defense, Atlanta sees motion on only 48% of snaps and is equally sound either way (−0.05 EPA with, −0.06 without).

Penix has turned the season around: +0.42 EPA per dropback on 46 dropbacks, completions 3.2 points above expectation (Next Gen Stats), 2 touchdowns, 1 interception, a 113.1 passer rating and one sack. Week 4 at New Orleans was his cleanest game, 15 of 20 for 223 yards and a touchdown (127.7 rating). Cooper Rush (−0.67 on 46) and Jack Strand (−0.60 on 19) still weigh on the team totals, which explains the 31st rank in passing EPA. Play action remains the best call (+0.58 EPA per dropback on 25 against −0.42 without).

Bijan Robinson is one of the best backs in the league: 494 yards at 5.8 per carry (3rd among qualifiers), 1.5 yards per carry over Next Gen Stats' expectation (2nd) and a 54% success rate. His 10 broken tackles through Week 3 rank 2nd behind Kenneth Walker (Pro Football Reference charting, which has not yet added the New Orleans game). Brian Robinson has been an efficient change of pace, +0.20 EPA per carry on 44 carries. Bijan's receiving has been low value, 14 catches for 120 yards at −0.33 EPA per target.

Drake London is the passing game: 20 catches on 25 targets for 370 yards, +0.93 EPA per target, 40% of the team's air yards and 2.1 yards after the catch above expectation. Jahan Dotson still gets the deep looks (14.9-yard average depth of target) but has caught 6 of 13 for −0.90 EPA per target. Kyle Pitts has 5 catches for 67 yards on 9 targets, and Austin Hooper has a touchdown among his 5 catches.

Through Week 3, Atlanta allowed pressure on 19% of dropbacks, 3rd lowest, and the sack rate has come down to 7.2% (23rd, from 26th) now that Penix is taking sacks on 2% of dropbacks. Bergeron and Neuzil have played every snap, Lindstrom 93% and Jawaan Taylor 90%, with Jake Matthews at 82%. Runs outside either end remain the best plays on the menu (10.9 yards per carry on 17 to the left end, 8.6 on 14 to the right), while runs behind right guard average 2.7.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, a measure that mostly reflects the QB) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Here it points at the earlier quarterbacks more than the line. Cooper Rush turned 5 of his 8 pressures into sacks (63%, 2nd highest; league 26%), while Penix took none on his first two and was sacked once at New Orleans, on a six-man blitz. Of the eight sacks, three came on a standard rush, three on blitzes, one was an extended play and one FTN charged to Rush.

The run defense leads the league, −0.25 EPA per rush allowed, and is best of all against light boxes (−0.41 EPA per run with six or fewer in the box). The rush gets there without finishing: 12.0 pressures per game through Week 3 ranks 5th, but the 3.7% sack rate is 27th. Cameron Thomas leads with 7 pressures and 8 QB hits, Za'Darius Smith has 2.5 sacks and 4 tackles for loss in part-time work, and Samson Ebukam adds 1.5 sacks and 7 QB hits.

11th in EPA per dropback allowed (from 14th). Coverage charting stops at Week 3, where the touchdowns were concentrated in two players: Mike Hughes allowed 13 catches for 221 yards and 3 touchdowns (137 passer rating), and Jessie Bates III allowed 4 touchdowns on 12 targets. C.J. Henderson has been the steadiest corner, with 6 passes defensed and an 81 rating allowed on 22 targets. Xavier Watts has the unit's interception and a forced fumble.

Through Week 3 (Pro Football Reference has not added the New Orleans game), Atlanta allowed a 98.5 passer rating in coverage (21st; league 93.2). Opponents completed just 56.8% of charted targets (5th lowest) but scored 9 touchdowns. Safeties were hit hardest, a 117.9 rating and 5 of the touchdowns on 30 targets; the corners were at 91.0 on 68 targets and the linebackers at 81.8, helped by Harold Perkins (5 of 11 for 34 yards).

Still a weak spot, 27th in special teams DVOA. Nick Folk is 6 of 9 on field goals with a long of 51 and perfect on 10 extra points. Jake Bailey nets 38.4 yards per punt with 7 of 13 inside the 20, and Zachariah Branch averages 13.8 yards on punt returns.

Still one of the league's best offenses, with a defense that has climbed to above average. Baltimore ranks 3rd in offensive EPA per play, 2nd in success rate and 2nd passing, scoring 29.0 points per game. The defense moved from 18th to 10th in EPA per play after holding Tennessee to −0.16 EPA per play in the 24–18 Week 4 win, and the run defense is up to 21st. The 3–1 record comes with a +20 point differential.
DVOA still has Baltimore 5th overall (21.3%), driven by the 3rd-ranked offense. The defense moved up from 15th to 12th, while special teams slipped to 25th.

Baltimore runs more than its situations would predict (9 points below expected pass rate, 6th-lowest) and has the 3rd most tight ends on the field. The defense plays more defensive backs than any team, 5.2 on average, so opponents see a light box on 66% of runs (league 45%). Sending five or more rushers (−0.09 EPA per dropback) still beats rushing four (+0.01), and Baltimore blitzes at about the league rate (31%).

Baltimore motions on 64% of snaps (7th; league 58%), and it has paid off in the run game: +0.14 EPA per run with motion against −0.24 without, the 2nd-biggest motion gain on runs. Passing is the reverse. Pass plays without motion (+0.59 EPA, 10.7 yards per play) have been far better than those with it (+0.20), the largest drop-off of any team. On defense, Baltimore is 7th against motion (−0.05 EPA per play).

Lamar Jackson ranks 3rd of 33 qualified quarterbacks in EPA per dropback (+0.38), with six touchdowns, one interception and completions 7.1 points above expectation (3rd). Week 4 was his most accurate game yet: 15 of 20 for 222 yards, two touchdowns and +9.6 CPOE against Tennessee. He still holds the ball longer than most (3.1 seconds, 5th slowest), and play action (30% of dropbacks, 6th most) remains slightly better than straight dropbacks, +0.39 vs. +0.34 EPA.

Derrick Henry has 374 yards on 89 carries (4.2 per carry, down from 4.6 through Week 3), still slightly above Next Gen Stats' expectation (+0.2 yards per carry, 15th of 46), with 209 of those yards after contact. His EPA per carry is just below break-even (−0.05) despite a 45% success rate. He has four broken tackles on runs and one after a catch (Pro Football Reference charting), Jackson has four on 19 carries, and the team ranks 10th in broken tackles per game.

Zay Flowers remains the big-play engine: 352 yards on 22 targets (16.0 per target), +1.09 EPA per target and 3.8 yards of YAC over expectation per catch, 3rd among 111 NGS-tracked receivers. Mark Andrews leads in targets (24%) on short routes (7.3-yard depth), and Rashod Bateman is the downfield option at a 13.0-yard depth and +0.73 EPA per target. Tight end Matthew Hibner has caught all five of his targets for 70 yards and a touchdown.

Pass protection has been among the league's best: Baltimore allows pressure on 20% of dropbacks (4th lowest), though the sack rate is middling (5.8%, 17th). John Simpson, Olaivavega Ioane and Roger Rosengarten have played every snap, while Ronnie Stanley (69%) and Jovaughn Gwyn (68%) have shared time with Carson Vinson (34%) and Emery Jones (15%). Runs average 2.7 yards before contact (11th), and runs off right end are still the most reliable at a 65% success rate. Linemen have drawn 13 accepted penalties, 29th in the league.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Jackson turns 29% of pressures into sacks, close to the league's 26% (16th highest of 36). FTN charged none of his seven sacks to him: three came against blitzes, two against a standard rush and two on extended plays.

Pass rush volume is still below average (7.8 pressures per game, 20th; league 9.3) and the sack rate ranks 24th. Tavius Robinson leads with seven pressures, two sacks and six QB hits, and Mike Green has six pressures and five QB hits in 43% of snaps. Trenton Simpson leads in tackles for loss (five) and Travis Jones has four. The run defense has improved from 27th to 21st in EPA per rush.

Pass defense jumped to 7th in EPA per dropback (from 15th). Roquan Smith has allowed a 39 passer rating with an interception, Trenton Simpson 37 with another, and Nate Wiggins has held 22 targets to 94 yards. Marlon Humphrey (215 yards on 23 targets) and safety Malaki Starks (9 of 10 for 151 yards, a 152 rating) are where opponents have found yards.

Baltimore's 92.4 passer rating allowed ranks 18th, close to the league's 93.2, with 89 of 139 targets completed for 1,032 yards. Linebackers have been the strength at 38.9 on 29 targets with both of the team's coverage interceptions (league 90.8 for linebackers). Safeties remain the weak spot at 120.1 and 10.8 yards per target (league 98.3), and two interceptions rank 20th.

Tyler Loop is 6 of 8 on field goals with a 64-yarder and perfect on 14 extra points. Chris Moore averages 28.6 yards on eight kick returns. Ryan Eckley nets 41.0 yards per punt with seven of 15 inside the 20, but special teams rank 25th in DVOA.

Buffalo is 3–1 after a 29–26 home loss to New England. The offense is still elite: 2nd in EPA per play, top four passing and rushing, and a league-high 31.8 points per game. The defense has slipped to 29th in EPA per play and 25th in points allowed (26.8 per game), and New England moved the ball for 407 yards. Seven giveaways, five of them in Week 3, are the other blemish.
DVOA puts Buffalo 4th overall, down from 3rd. The offense is 2nd, the defense has fallen to 26th, and special teams are 7th.

Buffalo uses more tight ends than any team (1.8 on the field on average, league 1.4) and fewer running backs than any. One-back sets are the engine at +0.31 EPA per play; empty sets take 11% of snaps, double the league rate, and have lost EPA (−0.16). On defense, the four-man rush allows +0.13 EPA per dropback, and sending five or more has been hit for +0.36 (league about zero).

Buffalo motions on 67% of snaps (5th; league 58%), yet it is the league's best offense without motion: +0.37 EPA per play, 1st, against +0.11 with it. The gap is widest on passes (+0.52 without, +0.19 with). On defense it has been better against motion, allowing +0.07 EPA per play with motion and +0.15 without.

Josh Allen ranks 5th of 33 qualified quarterbacks in EPA per dropback (+0.29), with six touchdowns, three interceptions and completions 2.2 points above Next Gen Stats' expectation. Against New England he was 23 of 33 for 253 yards with a touchdown and an interception. Play action is still less productive than straight dropbacks (+0.17 vs. +0.31 EPA), and blitzes haven't slowed him (+0.28 EPA when blitzed). He has a 65% success rate on his own carries.

James Cook has 421 yards on 70 carries (6.0 per carry), 3rd in the league, and 1.4 yards per carry over Next Gen Stats' expectation, 4th among 46 qualified backs. His seven broken tackles on runs are tied for 5th (Pro Football Reference charting). The blocking helps: Buffalo still leads the league in yards before contact per carry (3.5, league 2.4).

Keon Coleman has become the most efficient target, catching 14 of 16 for 217 yards at +1.12 EPA per target. Dalton Kincaid has 270 yards on 19 targets with 2.4 yards of YAC over expectation (10th of 111). Khalil Shakir leads in targets (23) and separation (4.0 yards, 8th) but has two drops and little after the catch, and DJ Moore draws 27% of the air yards on a 15.1-yard average depth of target.

The same five linemen have played every snap. Run blocking is the league's best by yards before contact, and runs behind left guard average 5.3 yards at +0.43 EPA. Pass protection has improved: Allen was sacked once against New England, and the sack rate is now 6.6% (19th, from 27th), with pressure on 22% of dropbacks (13th).

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. The blame still splits. Allen turns pressure into sacks a bit more often than average (30% vs. 26%), and FTN charged two of his nine sacks to him, with one more on an extended play. Four came against a standard rush, which points at protection, and the one in Week 4 came on a blitz.

The rush keeps producing volume: 13.8 pressures per game ranks 3rd (league 9.3), though the sack rate has dropped to 16th. Gregory Rousseau has 6 of the team's 10 sacks, 16 QB hits, 22 pressures, eight tackles for loss and three forced fumbles. Bradley Chubb adds seven QB hits and 10 pressures. The run defense ranks 22nd in EPA per rush.

Pass defense ranks 26th in EPA per dropback. Christian Benford (116 rating) and Maxwell Hairston (100.6) have each allowed two touchdowns on 20 targets. C.J. Gardner-Johnson remains the bright spot at safety, with an interception and a 47.5 rating allowed. Opponents have made six interception-worthy throws (league average 4.2).

Buffalo allows a 103.3 passer rating in coverage (26th; league 93.2): 93 of 149 for 1,160 yards, 10 touchdowns and two interceptions. Cornerbacks see 54% of targets (league 46%) and allow 101.9 (23rd). Linebackers are the weakest group at 112.0 (29th), with Dorian Williams allowing two touchdowns on 11 targets. Safeties are at 92.3 (13th).

Tyler Bass is 6 for 6 on field goals with a long of 46 and 13 of 14 on extra points. Greg Dortch averages 26.3 yards on 12 kick returns. Tommy Doman Jr. nets 45.0 yards on nine punts, four inside the 20. Special teams rank 7th in DVOA.

A 2–2 team that keeps outscoring its defense. Carolina ranks 8th in offensive EPA per play and 4th in points per game (30.3), but allows 27.3 per game (26th) and is 19th in defensive EPA. The 32–26 win over Detroit followed the pattern: +0.29 EPA per play and 449 yards on offense, 452 yards allowed. Both wins came with no giveaways, and Carolina is +3 in turnovers for the season.
DVOA has Carolina 9th overall (from 13th). The offense is up to 11th, the defense is still 18th, and special teams (5th) remain the best unit.

A pass-first, three-receiver offense: 2.5 wideouts per snap (11th most) and 3rd in pass rate over expected. Empty backfields (8% of plays, league 6%) have produced +0.63 EPA per play, and the two-back looks used on only 10% of snaps (league 20%) are at +0.18. The defense plays plenty of extra defensive backs (4.9 per snap, 6th most) and sends five or more on 36% of dropbacks, which has worked better than four rushers (−0.01 EPA per dropback against +0.11).

Carolina uses less motion than most (55% of plays, 21st; league 58%) but makes it count through the air: dropbacks with motion are at +0.31 EPA (3rd), against +0.14 without. Runs gain nothing from it (−0.12 with, −0.09 without). The defense is the problem against motion, allowing +0.07 EPA per play with it and −0.02 without; runs after motion average 5.5 yards against Carolina (31st) compared with 3.9 without.

Bryce Young keeps getting better: +0.23 EPA per dropback (9th of 33 qualifiers), completions 5.1 points above expectation (Next Gen Stats), 9 touchdowns, 2 interceptions and a 100.0 passer rating. FTN has charted one interception-worthy throw all season, among the fewest in the league. Week 4 against Detroit was his best game, 29 of 41 for 329 yards and 2 touchdowns, completions 8.5 points above expectation and a quicker 2.67-second release. He is still better when opponents don't blitz (+0.25 EPA per dropback against +0.17).

Chuba Hubbard is running 1.3 yards per carry over Next Gen Stats' expectation (5th of 46 qualifiers) at 5.0 yards per carry, and his 7 broken tackles (5 on runs) are tied for 5th in the league. He has also caught 10 of 11 targets for two touchdowns and +0.96 EPA per target. The backups have not helped: AJ Dillon (2.5 yards per carry, −0.56 EPA per carry) and Jonathon Brooks (3.3, −0.27) have combined for 26 carries. Carolina has slipped to tied for 8th in broken tackles per game (3.25).

Tetairoa McMillan has become the lead target, with 26 catches on 39 targets for 385 yards, two touchdowns, +0.41 EPA per target and a third of the team's air yards. Jalen Coker has been the most efficient (18 of 22, 222 yards, two touchdowns, +0.58 EPA per target) but had no targets in Week 4. Darren Waller has two touchdowns and 3.3 yards of separation, the most of any Panther, and Brycen Tremayne has added 115 yards on 9 targets.

Still a split verdict. Young is pressured on 34% of dropbacks, the highest rate in the league, but the 5.7% sack rate ranks 16th and the backs gain 2.9 yards before contact per carry, 5th best. Rasheed Walker, Robert Hunt and Luke Fortner have played nearly every snap, with Monroe Freeling at 88%. Runs behind left tackle average 8.0 yards; runs up the middle (3.0 yards, −0.24 EPA per carry) and to the right tackle and end (1.5 yards on 13 carries combined) are where the ground game stalls.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, a measure that mostly reflects the QB) plus FTN's charting of each sack. It splits the blame. Young turns pressure into sacks far less often than average (17% vs. 26%), so he escapes most of it, and FTN has charged none of his 10 sacks to him. But 6 of the 10 came against a standard four-man rush, which points at the line, and three more came on extended plays after he left the pocket, two of them against Detroit.

The pass rush has cooled: 11.0 pressures per game ranks 9th (from 4th) and the 4.8% sack rate is 22nd. Princely Umanmielen leads with 9 pressures, 3 sacks and 3 tackles for loss in under half the snaps, and Jaelan Phillips has 8 pressures and 2 sacks. Run defense is 20th in EPA per rush, and runs against light boxes (+0.14 EPA) are still where opponents hurt it.

17th against the pass (from 12th). Tre'von Moehrig has played 96% of the snaps and allowed a 59 passer rating, Lathan Ransom has allowed 2 catches on 11 targets, and Will Lee has 4 passes defensed with a 76 rating on a team-high 25 targets. The soft spots are Akayleb Evans (14 of 20 for 226 yards, 124 rating) and Jaycee Horn (108 rating). Devin Lloyd leads the defense with two interceptions from linebacker.

Still one of the better coverage units by passer rating, 84.5 allowed (7th; league 93.2), with opponents completing just 55.7% of charted targets (2nd lowest). The yards have crept up, though: 7.5 per target (17th, from 5th). The linebackers remain the strength, a 74.4 rating on 45 targets with all 3 interceptions (Lloyd 2, Bobby Okereke 1); the corners are at 97.7 and 8.7 yards per target, and the safeties at 79.6.

One of the league's better units (5th in special teams DVOA). Ryan Fitzgerald is 9 for 9 on field goals with a long of 53 but has missed 3 of 13 extra points. Sam Martin nets 43.2 yards per punt with 8 of 13 inside the 20.

Three straight wins have made Chicago a 3–1 team with a +47 differential, and the defense is the reason: 5th in EPA per play, 3rd against the pass, 4th in sack rate, and 28 points allowed in total across Weeks 2 through 4. The offense has not had to be great, only steady, and it is 9th in EPA per play and 8th in success rate having started three different quarterbacks. Week 4's 23–12 win over the Jets was the most lopsided yet by yardage, 495 to 157. The run defense, 26th in EPA per rush, is the one place this team can still be attacked.
DVOA has Chicago 8th overall at +17.0%, with the offense 9th (+12.2%) and the defense up to 6th (−7.4%). Special teams are the only below-average unit at 20th.

Chicago plays through tight ends more than almost anyone, averaging 1.75 on the field (2nd), with Colston Loveland at 87% of snaps and Cole Kmet at 65%. The defense is built on extra rushers: it sends five or more on 40% of dropbacks against a league rate of 31% and gets paid for it, −0.21 EPA per dropback with five or more against −0.07 with four. The counter is already showing up on the other side of the ball, where opponents have put eight or more in the box on 13% of Chicago's designed runs and held the offense to −0.54 EPA on those 18 runs.

Nobody in the league gets more out of moving a man, and nobody does it less. Chicago motions on 46.6% of snaps, 31st, but averages +0.25 EPA per play with motion against −0.02 without, a +0.27 swing that ranks 3rd, and its 55% success rate with motion is the best in football. The running game is the extreme version: +0.23 EPA and 6.2 yards a carry with motion against −0.22 and 3.8 without, the largest motion gain on the ground in the league. The defense sits on the wrong end of the same effect, allowing +0.03 EPA against motion and −0.13 without, and it faces the lowest motion rate in the league at 43.2%.

Three starters and no slippage. Caleb Williams was 4th among qualified passers at +0.31 EPA per dropback with completions 6.2 points above expectation before sitting out Weeks 3 and 4; he also held the ball 3.42 seconds, longer than any qualified passer. Case Keenum went +0.18 in his Week 3 start, and Tyson Bagent is at +0.11 after Week 4, with completions 9.1 points above expectation in that game. The oddest number is the blitz: Chicago faces one on 48% of dropbacks, the highest rate in the league, and is still slightly better against it (+0.26 EPA per dropback) than without it (+0.20).

Kyle Monangai has earned the better half of the split. He is at 5.4 yards per carry on 60 carries with +1.17 yards per carry over Next Gen Stats' expectation, 6th among qualified backs, and +0.10 EPA per carry; D'Andre Swift has 69 carries at 4.5 yards, sits essentially at expectation and is at −0.11 EPA. Both run behind good blocking, 2.96 yards before contact per carry (4th), and the Bears are 4th in broken tackles per game at 4.25, with Swift's six (Pro Football Reference charting) tied for 8th in the league.

The targets and the production have come apart. Luther Burden III leads with 29 targets but is at essentially zero EPA per target (+0.005) on 2.5 yards of separation. Rome Odunze is the explosive piece, 233 yards and 11.7 per target on a 14.9-yard average depth with 36% of the air yards, and he does it tight, 2.3 yards of separation, the least of the group, with two drops. Kalif Raymond is the efficiency outlier at 21 catches on 23 targets, +0.79 EPA per target and 4.3 yards of separation, 4th in the league. Loveland is the weak link at −0.27 EPA on 18 targets for 91 yards.

Darnell Wright, Garrett Bradbury, Joe Thuney and Jonah Jackson have played all 314 snaps, and Theo Benedet now takes the larger share at left tackle, 54% to Braxton Jones's 46%. The protection has improved to 21.1% pressure allowed (9th) with a 4.7% sack rate (11th). On the ground the right side is the plan and it half works: right guard is the most-used lane at 40 carries, +0.15 EPA and 4.3 yards, while right tackle (−0.37 on 24) and left guard (−0.47 on 24) are losses.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Chicago has allowed only seven sacks in four games. Williams was pressured on 34% of his dropbacks, well above the 23% league rate, but turned just 21% of that into sacks against a league figure of 26%. FTN charged none of the seven to a quarterback: three came on blitzes, two on standard rushes beaten and two on extended plays.

A rotation that finishes. Chicago is 12th in pressures per game at 10.0 against a 9.3 league average, but 4th in sack rate at 8.6% with 10 sacks. Dayo Odeyingbo leads with nine pressures, three sacks and three tackles for loss on 62% of snaps, Montez Sweat has seven pressures and two sacks, and Austin Booker has two sacks and four QB hits in a 54% role. None of it reaches the run defense, 26th in EPA per rush.

3rd in pass defense EPA, with a stark split inside the group. Rookie safety Dillon Thieneman has played every snap and allowed 4 of 12 for 50 yards with an interception, a 12.5 passer rating; Malik Muhammad is at 43.5 on 18 targets with an interception and a sack; T.J. Edwards has been excellent for a linebacker at 10 of 15 for a 53.8 rating with an interception. The corners are where everything goes: Jaylon Johnson has allowed 15 of 18 for 248 yards, and Tyrique Stevenson 192 yards and three touchdowns on 15 targets.

Chicago has allowed an 87.1 passer rating in coverage (9th; league 93.2), only 819 yards (4th fewest) and four touchdowns (3rd fewest), on 24.5 targets a game. The middle of the field is shut: linebackers 51.4, 2nd in the league on 25 targets, and safeties 71.0. The cornerbacks are the hole at 111.5 on 51 targets, 11.0 yards per target and three of the four touchdowns, which is why the defense still ranks 25th in yards allowed per target at 8.4 despite everything else.

Cairo Santos is 7 of 8 on field goals with a long of 50 and 13 for 13 on extra points. Tory Taylor has punted only eight times, a 43.3-yard net with three inside the 20. Zavion Thomas averages 21.3 yards per kickoff return and Kalif Raymond 10.5 per punt return. DVOA still puts the unit 20th, and seven special-teams penalties (25th), three of them Santos kickoffs short of the landing zone, are part of why.

Back to 2–2 after a 22–17 home loss to Jacksonville in which Cincinnati outgained the Jaguars 437 to 325 but turned it over twice and ran for −0.31 EPA per carry. The offense ranks 10th in EPA per play and the defense 11th, both down from a week ago (9th and 5th). After a dominant start, the defense has allowed positive EPA per play in each of the last two games.
DVOA dropped Cincinnati from 7th to 11th (10.6%). The offense holds at 10th, but the defense fell from 11th to 21st, and special teams are 12th.

Cincinnati passes more than its situations would predict (9 points over expected pass rate, 2nd highest). The defense still blitzes less than anyone, sending extra rushers on 16% of dropbacks (league 31%), and when it does it has been very effective (−0.37 EPA per dropback). The four-man rush, used on 80% of dropbacks, has given up +0.14. On offense, Cincinnati sees heavy boxes (8 or more) on 20% of runs, about double the league rate, and those runs have averaged −0.37 EPA.

Cincinnati motions less than most (52% of snaps, 24th; league 58%), and its offense has been much better without it: +0.17 EPA per play without motion against −0.05 with, a gap that ranks 27th. The split holds for passes (+0.23 vs. about zero) and runs (−0.03 vs. −0.13). On defense, motion has hurt Cincinnati against the pass (+0.08 EPA per pass play vs. −0.08 without) but helped against the run (−0.20 vs. +0.10).

Joe Burrow ranks 15th of 33 qualified quarterbacks in EPA per dropback (+0.12), with seven touchdowns and three interceptions. He is accurate (4.5 points over expected completion rate, 10th) in a quick, short game: 2.6 seconds to throw (2nd fastest) and a 7.3-yard average depth of target. Week 4 asked much more of him, 54 attempts for 428 yards with one touchdown and two interceptions. Blitzes and play action still hurt: −0.13 EPA per dropback when blitzed against +0.21 when not, and −0.08 on play action, which Cincinnati uses on only 17% of dropbacks (30th).

Chase Brown is averaging 3.6 yards per carry, 0.6 below Next Gen Stats' expectation (41st of 46 qualified backs), with −0.11 EPA per carry and a 38% success rate. Only 75 of his 207 yards have come after contact. He has three broken tackles on runs and two after catches (Pro Football Reference charting), and the team ranks 22nd in broken tackles per game. He is also heavily targeted (21 catches on 24 targets) but averages 4.3 yards per target and −0.27 EPA.

Tee Higgins has become the focal point: 39 targets (25%), 46% of the team's air yards and 401 yards at +0.63 EPA per target on a 13.3-yard average depth. Ja'Marr Chase has 28 targets, 212 yards and three touchdowns on shorter routes (8.4-yard depth). Mike Gesicki is the most efficient option, with three touchdowns on 15 targets and +1.02 EPA per target, and Dohnte Meyers gets 4.2 yards of separation, 6th among 111 NGS-tracked receivers.

The most stable line in the division: Orlando Brown Jr., Dylan Fairchild, Ted Karras and Dalton Risner have played every snap and Amarius Mims all but three. Burrow's quick release keeps the sack rate at 5.3% (14th) while pressure arrives on 24% of dropbacks (20th). Run blocking ranks 18th in yards before contact (2.4 per carry), and the few runs off left and right tackle have averaged 1.8 and 0.8 yards. Fairchild has four accepted penalties, three for holding.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Burrow converts 22% of pressures into sacks, below the league's 26% (22nd highest of 36). FTN charged two of his nine sacks to him, and six came against a standard four-man rush, including both in Week 4, so the sacks that do happen lean toward protection.

Still a four-man rush that gets home: 11.5 pressures per game (6th; league 9.3) and the 3rd-best sack rate. Dexter Lawrence leads with three sacks, eight pressures and six QB hits, Jonathan Allen has two sacks and eight pressures, and Boye Mafe has two sacks and four tackles for loss. Kris Jenkins and Cedric Johnson have two sacks each in part-time roles. The run defense ranks 14th in EPA per rush.

Pass defense slipped to 10th in EPA per dropback (from 7th). Daxton Hill remains the anchor, allowing a 68 passer rating on 23 targets with five passes defensed, and DJ Turner has four passes defensed. Linebacker coverage is still the leak: Demetrius Knight has allowed 16 of 21 for 188 yards (a 119 rating) and Barrett Carter 172 yards on 23 targets.

Opponents keep throwing at Cincinnati (154 charted targets, 4th most) and have piled up 1,259 yards (29th) at 8.2 yards per target (23rd). The 90.8 passer rating allowed ranks 15th, helped by only four touchdowns (3rd fewest). Corners have held up (82.0 on 69 targets, 51% completed), while linebackers allow 101.6 on 45 targets (league 90.8), and one interception in coverage ranks 25th.

Evan McPherson is 9 for 9 on field goals with a long of 58 and perfect on 10 extra points. Dohnte Meyers averages 26.5 yards on 13 kick returns, and Ryan Rehkow nets 39.2 yards per punt with seven of 13 inside the 20. Special teams rank 12th in DVOA.

3–1 after a 27–24 win over Pittsburgh, but still outscored by 14 on the season. The offense has climbed from 22nd to 16th in EPA per play on a passing game that ranks 13th, while the run game is 31st. The defense is 18th. Week 4 was Cleveland's best offensive game of the season (+0.10 EPA per play, 374 yards).
DVOA still rates Cleveland well below its record, but it moved from 27th to 24th (−10.0%). The offense improved from 29th to 25th and the defense from 19th to 16th, and special teams hold at 8th.

Cleveland passes more than any team relative to its situations (10 points over expected pass rate, 1st). Two-back sets (21% of snaps) remain costly at −0.30 EPA per play, while one-back sets are near break-even. The defense blitzes on 24% of dropbacks (24th; league 31%) and plays light boxes against 71% of runs; the four-man rush allows +0.09 EPA per dropback and five or more −0.12.

Cleveland motions on just 52% of snaps (26th), but it has worked: +0.08 EPA per play with motion against −0.13 without, the 6th-biggest gain. The effect is largest on passes, +0.33 EPA per pass play with motion (2nd) against −0.02 without. On defense it's the opposite: Cleveland allows +0.16 EPA per pass play against motion (26th) and −0.11 without.

Deshaun Watson has climbed to 13th of 33 qualified quarterbacks in EPA per dropback (+0.14), with six touchdowns and two interceptions. Completions are still below expectation (−2.6 points by NGS), and the passing game is very short, with his average throw landing 2.9 yards short of the sticks. Play action hasn't helped (−0.06 EPA per dropback vs. +0.20 without), but blitzes no longer bother him: +0.14 when blitzed and +0.15 when not, against a 36% blitz rate (8th highest).

Quinshon Judkins is still breaking tackles without finding room: 3.0 yards per carry, 0.5 below Next Gen Stats' expectation, a 27% success rate and −0.29 EPA per carry. His seven broken tackles (five on runs, two after catches) are tied for 5th in the league (Pro Football Reference charting), and 94 of his 177 rushing yards came after contact. Cleveland ranks 31st in yards before contact per carry (1.6), so most of the problem is up front.

Denzel Boston is the big-play threat: 51% of the team's air yards on a 17.8-yard average depth (4th deepest among 111 NGS-tracked receivers), 284 yards, two touchdowns and 4.3 yards of YAC over expectation (2nd). Harold Fannin Jr. gets 5.8 yards of separation, the most of any tracked receiver, and has three touchdowns on 23 targets. KC Concepcion still leads with 28 targets but has 144 yards and −0.04 EPA per target.

The line has barely changed: Austin Barber, Spencer Fano, Zion Johnson and Tytus Howard have played virtually every snap, with Elgton Jenkins (74%) and Luke Wypler (26%) at the fifth spot. Cleveland is 31st in yards before contact (1.6 per carry), and runs off left end have averaged 0.9 yards. Pressure is down to 21% of dropbacks (8th lowest), but the sack rate is still 7.9% (25th). Howard has five false starts, part of 12 accepted line penalties (27th).

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Watson still turns pressure into sacks more than most: 38% (7th highest of 36; league 26%). FTN charged five of his 11 sacks to him, including both in Week 4, three more came against blitzes and one on an extended play, leaving only two where a standard rush beat the line.

Mason Graham still leads with four sacks, five QB hits and six tackles for loss. Cleveland sacked Aaron Rodgers five times in Week 4, and the sack rate has risen to 9th, though pressure volume is modest (7.8 per game, 20th; league 9.3). The run defense ranks 23rd in EPA per rush. Front-seven players have drawn 11 accepted penalties, 32nd in the league.

Pass defense is 14th in EPA per dropback. Grant Delpit has been the best cover player (a 52 passer rating, an interception and a sack), and Mekhi Blackmon has held 17 targets to 91 yards. Denzel Ward has allowed only 10 catches on 26 targets but three touchdowns, as has Ronnie Hickman, while Myles Harden (230 yards) and Tyson Campbell (179 yards on 12 targets) have been the most costly.

Opponents complete only 56% of targets against Cleveland (2nd lowest) and four interceptions rank 4th, but 10 touchdowns allowed rank 28th, leaving the passer rating at 89.9 (13th; league 93.2). Safeties (84.4 on 44 targets) have been slightly better than corners (91.5 on 82), and linebackers have allowed 96.5 on 27.

Still a strength, 8th in DVOA. Andre Szmyt is 8 for 8 on field goals with a long of 56. Corey Bojorquez nets 46.8 yards per punt with seven of 16 inside the 20, and Raheim Sanders averages 29.3 yards on 10 kick returns.

Dallas is 2–2 after a 34–30 win at Houston, with a +10 point differential. The offense ranks 6th in EPA per play and 2nd in scoring at 30.5 points per game, while the defense is last in both EPA per play and success rate and allows 28.0 points per game (28th). Turnovers are still even at two each, so the losses keep coming back to a defense that can't get off the field.
DVOA agrees with EPA. Dallas is 13th overall, with the 6th-ranked offense, the 32nd-ranked defense (down from 27th) and 6th-ranked special teams.

Dallas stays a three-receiver offense: one back on 80% of snaps (league 74%) at +0.16 EPA per play, and 2.7 receivers on the field on average (league 2.4). The defense rushes four on 71% of dropbacks and gives up +0.62 EPA per dropback on those snaps, against a league +0.10. Sending five or more has been far better (+0.07), but FTN has Dallas blitzing on 27% of dropbacks, below the 31% league rate.

Dallas motions on 54% of snaps (22nd; league 58%) and has been better without it: +0.22 EPA per play without motion (4th) against +0.11 with it, and runs after motion average just 2.5 yards. On defense the motion gap is the largest in the league. Opponents motion on 65% of snaps (6th most) and average +0.35 EPA per play when they do, last in the league, against −0.08 without (8th).

Dak Prescott is still one of the most productive passers: +0.26 EPA per dropback (7th of 33 qualified), completions 5.5 points above expectation, eight touchdowns against one interception and a 3.6% team sack rate (6th). He went 32 of 45 for 335 yards and a touchdown at Houston. The soft spots haven't changed: +0.13 EPA per dropback against the blitz vs. +0.32 without, and +0.11 on play action vs. +0.31 without.

Javonte Williams has 62 of the backs' 76 carries at 3.7 yards per carry, almost exactly Next Gen Stats' expectation (+0.04) and break-even by EPA (−0.01). Blocking is about average, 2.6 yards before contact per carry (14th; league 2.4). He has three broken tackles on runs and the team has nine in all, 17th per game (Pro Football Reference charting). He has also caught 15 of 17 targets with a touchdown.

CeeDee Lamb has the best EPA per target (+0.91) of any receiver with 40 or more targets: 37 catches on 46 targets for 498 yards and four touchdowns, with 46% of the team's air yards. George Pickens has 18 catches on 28 targets for 225 yards, no touchdowns and three drops. Jake Ferguson has three touchdowns on 12 catches, almost all short looks (4.5-yard depth of target, 3.9 yards of separation).

Tyler Guyton, T.J. Bass, Cooper Beebe, Tyler Booker and Terence Steele have played every snap but one. Pressure has crept up to 24.5% of dropbacks (24th; league 23.3%), but the sack rate is still a strong 3.6% (6th). The run game stays lopsided: runs behind left tackle average 9.0 yards and +0.50 EPA, while runs behind right tackle average 0.9 yards and −0.48 EPA.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. For Dallas it's a small problem. Only 6 of Prescott's 41 pressures became sacks (15% vs. a 26% league rate). FTN charged four of the six to him, including one of the three at Houston; the other two that day were a rush won and an extended play.

The pass rush is still the root of the defensive problem: 7.8 pressure credits per game (20th; league 9.3) and four sacks, a 3.1% sack rate that ranks 29th. Donovan Ezeiruaku leads with seven pressures, ahead of Quinnen Williams and Rashan Gary with five each. The run defense is middling at 16th in EPA per rush, and Williams and Jaishawn Barham have four tackles for loss apiece.

Dallas is 32nd in pass defense EPA. DaRon Bland has allowed 15 of 21 for 182 yards and two touchdowns (a 129.5 rating), and the linebackers are getting picked on underneath: Jaishawn Barham has allowed 11 of 11 and Dee Winters 11 of 12. Shavon Revel (7 of 15, 62.9 rating) and Cobie Durant (1 of 5) have been the best corners, and Caleb Downs has two forced fumbles and a sack from safety.

Dallas now has the worst coverage numbers in the league: a 127.5 passer rating allowed (32nd), 74.5% completions (32nd) and still no interceptions. Cornerbacks are at 114.1 on 51 targets against a league 93.3. The middle of the field is worse: linebackers have allowed 27 of 28 for a 124.0 rating, and safeties a 145.8 rating with three touchdowns on 27 targets (league 98.3).

Dallas ranks 6th in special teams DVOA. Brandon Aubrey is 8 of 11 on field goals with a long of 60 and has missed one extra point. KaVontae Turpin averages 28.1 yards on 15 kickoff returns and 11.3 on punt returns. Bryan Anger has punted only seven times, five inside the 20.

2–2 with a −20 point differential after a 14–24 loss at San Francisco. The offense ranks 20th in EPA per play and 24th in success rate and scores 18.5 points per game (27th). The defense is 23rd in EPA per play: 15th against the pass, but 31st against the run.
DVOA still calls Denver average: 14th overall, with the 15th-ranked offense, the 14th-ranked defense and special teams at 15th.

Denver is still a one-back offense (81% of snaps); two-back looks (16%) are at −0.11 EPA per play. The defense blitzes on 39% of dropbacks (6th; league 31%), but the payoff has faded: five or more rushers now allow +0.05 EPA per dropback on 61 plays, the same as four-man rushes. Runs into eight-man boxes have gashed Denver for +0.57 EPA per carry on 18 plays.

Denver motions on 56% of plays (18th; league 58%). Motion helps the passing game (+0.08 EPA per dropback with it, −0.13 without) but not the run game, where runs after motion succeed 31% of the time against 58% without. On defense the problem is plays without motion: offenses average 8.3 yards per play (32nd) and +0.19 EPA (30th) when they line up still against Denver, including 7.7 yards per carry on runs.

Bo Nix is at −0.03 EPA per dropback (24th of 33 qualifiers) and completing 5.3% below Next Gen Stats' expectation (31st). His average intended target is 6.2 yards downfield, 2.8 yards short of the sticks, and FTN has charted 7 interception-worthy throws (4th-most; league average 4.2) to go with 5 touchdowns and 3 interceptions. Play action helps (+0.18 EPA per dropback against −0.07), and the blitz still hurts (−0.30 when blitzed against +0.13).

J.K. Dobbins has 46 carries at 3.5 yards per carry, −0.17 EPA per carry and a 26% success rate, 0.64 yards below Next Gen Stats' expectation (42nd of 46). Denver's running backs still have no broken tackles on runs (Pro Football Reference), and the team's 4 broken tackles rank 28th per game. RJ Harvey has caught 20 of 21 targets, and Jonah Coleman has 39 yards on 10 carries.

Jaylen Waddle leads with 26 targets and 37% of the air yards, catching 16 for 185 yards with 4.0 yards of separation, but has 3 drops. Courtland Sutton is the drag: 9 catches on 22 targets, 3.9 yards per target and −0.52 EPA per target on a 12.3-yard average depth. Pat Bryant (9 of 12, 133 yards, +1.03 EPA per target) and tight end Nate Adkins (2 touchdowns on 5 targets) remain the efficient options.

The same five linemen (Bolles, Powers, Wattenberg, Meinerz, McGlinchey) have played essentially every snap. Nix is pressured on 22% of dropbacks (16th) but sacked on just 3.5% (5th), and only once since Week 1. Run blocking is the weak spot: 2.1 yards before contact per carry (25th), with no standout lane; right guard (+0.13 EPA on 10 carries) is the best and left tackle (−0.28 on 6) the worst.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Nix rarely lets pressure become a sack (16% vs. 26% league; 6th-lowest of 36), and he has been sacked once since Week 1. FTN charted his 5 sacks as 2 standard rushes, 1 blitz, 1 extended play and 1 charged to him.

Zach Allen is still the engine: 13 pressures, 3 sacks and 12 QB hits. Nik Bonitto (5 pressures, a sack) and Malcolm Roach (4 pressures, 3 tackles for loss) are next. As a unit Denver is below average at getting home (8.5 pressure credits per game, 18th; sack rate 20th), and the run defense is 31st in EPA per rush allowed.

15th in pass defense EPA. Talanoa Hufanga has allowed 5 catches on 13 targets for 54 yards with 2 interceptions and an 11.9 rating. Patrick Surtain II has allowed 9 of 18 with no touchdowns (68.5 rating). Riley Moss has allowed 3 touchdowns but has 5 passes defensed, and Ja'Quan McMillian has given up 156 yards on 15 targets.

Denver has allowed an 83.5 passer rating in coverage (6th; league 93.2), and opponents complete just 58% of their throws (7th). The safeties have 3 of the 4 interceptions and a 61.1 rating allowed, though Brandon Jones has given up 161 yards on 12 targets. Linebackers see a third of the targets (45), led by Alex Singleton (23, 84.1 rating), and the cornerbacks have allowed 4 of the 6 touchdowns.

Wil Lutz is 5 of 7 on field goals with a long of 52 and 5 of 5 on extra points. Jeremy Crawshaw averages 49.7 yards per punt (45.3 net) on 19 punts, 9 inside the 20. RJ Harvey averages 29.2 yards per kickoff return. DVOA ranks the unit 15th.

Four games in, Detroit is the most lopsided team in the league: 7th in offensive EPA per play and 4th in success rate, 31st in defensive EPA per play. It scores 29.75 points a game (5th) and allows 31.75 (31st), which nets out to 2–2 and a −8 differential. The pattern does not vary much either — 449 yards allowed at Buffalo in Week 2, 449 again at Carolina in Week 4, where 452 yards of offense and no takeaways still produced a 32–26 loss. A +3 turnover margin is holding the record up.

DVOA has Detroit 16th overall at −1.0%, with the 8th-ranked offense (+12.3%) and the 30th-ranked defense (+16.2%); special teams are 13th. The 22-place gap between the two units' ranks is the 4th-widest in the league.

The offense is a one-back, play-action team and comfortable there: 82% of snaps with a single back at +0.20 EPA per play, and play action on 30% of dropbacks against a 24% league rate. Empty sets have been abandoned for cause, −0.53 EPA on 12 plays. On defense the dial does not matter: +0.26 EPA per dropback against four rushers, +0.29 against five or more, +0.50 on the nine snaps with three or fewer. Opponents have dropped back 189 times against Detroit, more than against any other defense.

Detroit is one of the few offenses that is better standing still: +0.20 EPA per play without motion against +0.09 with it, a −0.11 gap that ranks 22nd, and the passing game falls from +0.34 to +0.15 when a man moves. It motions on 50.9% of snaps, 28th. The running game is the exception, slightly better with motion by EPA (−0.02 against −0.07) though worse by yards (3.8 against 4.9). The defense is beaten either way and worse against motion, +0.21 EPA per play (31st) against +0.16 without, while seeing motion on 57.8% of opponent snaps.

Jared Goff is the most reliable part of this team: +0.24 EPA per dropback (8th among qualified passers), nine touchdowns and no interceptions in four games, a 108.6 passer rating and a 4.6% sack rate. Week 4 was his busiest and least efficient day, 32 of 52 for 412 yards with completions 6.2 points below expectation and his deepest average target of the year at 10.2 yards. He is better blitzed (+0.34 EPA per dropback) than not (+0.19) and gets the ball out in 2.83 seconds, so the pressure he does see is rarely his own doing.

Jahmyr Gibbs is the backfield: 80 of the team's 89 running back carries, 4.4 yards each at essentially Next Gen Stats' expectation (+0.05), plus 22 catches for 187 yards and two touchdowns on 28 targets. His nine broken tackles (Pro Football Reference charting) are 4th in the league, though they come on 102 touches, the heaviest workload of anyone in the top 10. The blocking is fine at 2.91 yards before contact per carry (6th); what is missing is anything after contact, and the team's rushing EPA sits 14th.

Amon-Ra St. Brown has the volume without the efficiency: 46 targets (29% share), 31 catches, 303 yards and five touchdowns, but 6.6 yards per target and 0.45 yards of YAC below expectation. Sam LaPorta is the most efficient regular at +0.58 EPA per target with 3.5 yards of separation, 25th in the league. Isaac TeSlaa has become a genuine second deep option, 17 targets for 187 yards at 11.0 per target on a 14.5-yard average depth with 3.9 yards of separation. Jameson Williams takes the same deep role and has four of the team's seven drops and no touchdowns on 25 targets.

Penei Sewell, Juice Scruggs and Tate Ratledge have played all 278 snaps alongside Goff, Blake Miller has 77% at the other tackle, and left guard is still a three-way rotation among Christian Mahogany (53%), Ben Bartch (47%) and Larry Borom (33%). The protection is genuinely good: 19.6% pressure allowed, 5th-lowest, and a 4.6% sack rate (10th). Runs up the middle are the most-used and most reliable lane, 29 carries at 4.0 yards and a 59% success rate. The discipline is the problem, 13 offensive line penalties, 29th in the league, eight of them false starts.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Goff is pressured on only 19.6% of dropbacks, 5th-lowest, and converts it to a sack 23.5% of the time against a 25.9% league rate. The eight sacks are concentrated: four are the ones FTN charged to Goff himself at Buffalo in Week 2, two were Jets blitzes in Week 3, and two were standard rushes beaten in Weeks 1 and 4.

The pass rush is the one working part of the defense: 12.75 pressures per game (4th; league 9.3) and 15 sacks at a 7.9% rate (6th). Aidan Hutchinson has 13 pressures, nine QB hits, 3.5 sacks and three tackles for loss on 89% of snaps; Alim McNeill has three sacks and four tackles for loss, D.J. Wonnum three sacks, and Derrick Barnes two plus an interception. Four games of a top-five rush have done nothing for the run defense, 27th in EPA per rush.

29th in pass defense EPA, and the trouble is everywhere rather than anywhere. D.J. Reed has allowed 248 yards and two touchdowns on 21 targets (134.6 rating), Roger McCreary 164 yards and a touchdown on 15 (131.0), Avonte Maddox 158 yards and two touchdowns on 11 (139.2), and Thomas Harper 128 yards on eight (145.8). Chuck Clark is the exception, 7 of 16 for a 43.0 rating with an interception, a sack and a forced fumble, and Derrick Barnes (56.9) is the other.

Detroit has allowed 1,584 coverage yards, the most in the league, on 45.3 targets a game, with 11 touchdowns (30th), a 106.2 passer rating (29th) and only two interceptions. No group is better than average: cornerbacks 117.0 (30th), safeties 107.7 (20th), linebackers 94.0 (17th). Jack Campbell is the most-targeted Lions defender at 18 of 28 for 228 yards and two touchdowns, and the four touchdowns allowed by the safeties are the other half of the problem. Opponents are not even being efficient about it, completing 62.4% (16th); there is simply no part of the field that is closed.

Jake Bates is perfect, 7 for 7 on field goals with a long of 54 and 14 for 14 on extra points. Jack Fox has a 42.1-yard net on 15 punts with six inside the 20. Jacob Saylors (25.4 yards) and Tom Kennedy (24.8) split kickoff returns and Kennedy adds 11.5 per punt return. The unit is 13th in DVOA and the least-penalized part of the team, three flags in four games (7th).

The 17–14 win at Tampa Bay got Green Bay to 2–2, and nothing underneath it has changed: 25th in offensive EPA per play, 27th in success rate, and last in the league in EPA per rush. The defense is 21st overall and 24th against the run. At 18.25 points a game (28th) against 26.25 allowed, and with a −32 differential and a −2 turnover margin, this is still a team whose record is better than its play. Its two wins came by three points each.
DVOA is harsher than the record: 27th overall at −20.7%, with the offense 28th (−18.6%) and the defense 24th (+5.4%). Special teams (11th) are the only above-average unit.

The Packers are in one-back sets on 82% of snaps and those plays are at −0.12 EPA, while the small two-back (29 plays) and empty (13) samples are both positive. Play action is used on 16.1% of dropbacks, 31st in the league against a 24% average, and it is worth +0.26 EPA per dropback against −0.02 without — the most obvious unused lever on the team. The telling defensive number is what opponents do: they play a light box on 70% of Green Bay's designed runs, the kind of invitation most offenses punish, and Green Bay is at −0.31 EPA on those 49 runs.

Motion is the second unused lever. Green Bay averages −0.01 EPA per play with it against −0.20 without, a +0.18 swing that ranks 7th, and the running game goes from 2.1 yards a carry without motion to 4.2 with it, yet the motion rate is only 58.2%, right at the 58.4% league average. On defense it sees more motion than almost anyone, 69.3% of snaps (2nd) and 80.9% of opponent runs (1st), and it actually handles motion runs better (−0.07 EPA) than static ones (+0.17), so the volume is not hurting it.

Jordan Love has taken every dropback and sits at +0.03 EPA per dropback (19th among qualified passers) with eight touchdowns and three interceptions. His completion rate is 7.0 points below expectation, 31st of 33 qualified passers, and FTN has charted six interception-worthy throws, tied for 5th-most. Two things complicate the picture: his receivers have dropped 11 passes, the most in the league, and Week 4 was his first game above expectation (+1.6) and his best rating of the year at 98.9. He is also the quickest-releasing qualified passer in the league at 2.48 seconds, and much worse blitzed (−0.22 EPA per dropback) than not (+0.20), on a 41% blitz rate that is 3rd-highest.

The worst running game in the league by EPA, and it is not close. MarShawn Lloyd is at 2.7 yards per carry on 30 carries, −1.46 yards per carry against Next Gen Stats' expectation — last among all 46 qualified backs — and −0.42 EPA per carry. Kaleb Johnson has four broken tackles on 20 carries, the one encouraging number in the group, but is at −0.46 EPA; Chris Brooks is the most efficient of the three at 4.7 yards on 15 carries. The blocking is the root cause: 1.75 yards before contact per carry, 30th, and all eight run lanes carry negative EPA, with the most-used (up the middle, 20 carries) at 2.6 yards.

Christian Watson is the one receiver winning: 20 catches for 331 yards and four touchdowns, 10.3 yards per target and +3.5 yards of YAC above expectation, 5th in the league, on only 2.5 yards of separation — a make-your-own-yards profile. Matthew Golden has the volume and the air yards (37 targets, 39% of them, a 14.4-yard average depth) but just 18 catches and four drops. Tucker Kraft is useful on short routes at +0.15 EPA per target with 3.3 yards of separation but has three drops of his own, and Skyy Moore wins 4.2 yards of separation (5th) and does nothing with it, 35 yards on 13 targets.

Still unsettled four games in. Jordan Morgan and Sean Rhyan have played all 253 snaps alongside Love, Anthony Belton and Jacob Monk are at 74% each, and six more linemen have taken snaps in the remaining spots. Pressure comes on 24.1% of dropbacks (21st), though the sack rate is a tolerable 4.9% (13th), partly because Love gets rid of it so fast. In the run game there is nothing to build on, with every lane negative and 11 offensive line penalties on top.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Love is pressured often, 24.1% of dropbacks, and converts it to a sack less than average, 20.5% against 25.9%. The split by cause is clean: four of the eight were Minnesota blitzes in Week 1, and of the four since, FTN charged three to Love himself, two of those on scrambles out of the pocket. The blitz plan beat the line early; the recent ones are the quarterback's.

A rush that gets there and does not finish: 10.25 pressures per game (11th) and 10 sacks at a 7.2% rate (11th). Lukas Van Ness leads with eight pressures, six QB hits, 2.5 sacks and four tackles for loss, and Edgerrin Cooper has three sacks, six tackles for loss and an interception from linebacker on 83% of snaps. Green Bay blitzes on 40% of dropbacks, 4th-most, and gets nothing extra for it (+0.06 EPA per dropback with five or more, +0.11 with four). The run defense is 24th in EPA per rush.

21st in pass defense EPA, carried entirely by the safeties. Xavier McKinney and Evan Williams have both played all 273 snaps and both have interceptions, with Williams allowing 6 of 14 for 55 yards (48.2 rating) and adding five pressures and a sack. Keisean Nixon has handled the heaviest volume in the division (19 of 29 for 175 yards, no touchdowns, one interception, 67.5) and Javon Bullard 9 of 15 for 63. Brandon Cisse is the hole: 181 yards and two touchdowns on 14 targets for a 153.3 rating, on 90% of snaps.

Green Bay has allowed a 90.4 passer rating in coverage (14th; league 93.2), four interceptions (tied 4th-most) and only 863 yards (5th fewest). The shape is unusual: opponents complete 66.4% of their throws, 29th, but gain only 7.3 yards per target, 10th, so the defense concedes the easy stuff and wins on the splash plays. The safeties are the strength at 69.5 on 40 targets (6th) and the linebackers are fine at 87.5; the cornerbacks sit 26th at 106.4, almost all of it Cisse.

Trey Smack is 6 of 7 on field goals with a long of 59 but has missed an extra point. Daniel Whelan has been both busy and excellent: 18 punts, a 44.4-yard net, 12 inside the 20. Skyy Moore averages 16.0 yards per punt return and 27.5 per kickoff return, and the unit is 11th in DVOA. The penalties undo a lot of it — 42 for 344 yards, 10.5 and 86 a game, 31st and 32nd in the league, with 12 giving opponents a first down (29th) and eight flags on the defensive backs.

Still winless at 0–4, but the offense finally showed up in Week 4 with 397 yards and +0.24 EPA per play in a 30–34 home loss to Dallas. Over four games the offense is 17th in EPA per play while the run game is 30th, and the defense has slipped to 22nd in EPA per play despite ranking 5th in success rate. Three of the four losses came by five points or fewer, and Houston allows 27.3 points per game (26th).
DVOA still sees an average team rather than a winless one. Houston is 17th overall (−2.4%), with the 13th-ranked offense, the 15th-ranked defense and special teams at 28th.

Still a one-back offense (80% of snaps, league 74%), and its runs into seven-man boxes, 59% of designed runs, have cost −0.29 EPA each. On defense Houston fields the third-most defensive backs in the league (4.98 per snap) and blitzes on just 21% of dropbacks (league 31%); the four-man rush has allowed +0.13 EPA per dropback. Light-box run defense remains good at −0.15 EPA per run.

Houston uses presnap motion on 56% of plays (19th; league 58%), and it has mattered more here than almost anywhere. With motion the offense averages +0.08 EPA per play against −0.16 without, the 4th-largest gain in the league, nearly all of it through the air (+0.25 vs. −0.19 per pass play). Runs with motion are the exception at −0.33 EPA per carry (31st). On defense Houston has seen motion on only 45% of snaps, second-least in the league, and its run defense against it is the league's best (−0.30 EPA per run).

C.J. Stroud had his best game in Week 4: 21 of 31 for 347 yards and 2 touchdowns, completing 14.3% above expectation by Next Gen Stats. That lifts him to +0.09 EPA per dropback (17th of 33 qualifiers) and 5.3% CPOE (7th), still with no interceptions in four games. He still holds the ball a long time (3.01 seconds, league 2.90) and throws into tight windows 20.5% of the time (league 15.0%). Play action has been a big help, +0.36 EPA per dropback on 36 plays against −0.01 without.

The run game hasn't recovered. David Montgomery is at 2.7 yards per carry and −0.34 EPA per carry on 47 carries, and both he and Woody Marks are running below Next Gen Stats' expectation (−0.31 and −0.49 yards per carry, 32nd and 37th of 46 qualifiers). Houston has 7 broken tackles in four games (Marks 3 and Montgomery 3 on runs, Jared Wayne 1 after a catch), 22nd per game in Pro Football Reference charting.

Dalton Schultz is still the most-targeted player (27 targets, 20% share) and a reliable outlet: 21 catches for 214 yards, +0.26 EPA per target and 4.0 yards of separation. Nico Collins has turned 18 targets into 14 catches, 193 yards, 3 touchdowns and +0.80 EPA per target despite averaging just 1.8 yards of separation. Xavier Hutchinson still draws the most air yards (27% share) but has caught only 12 of 26, and Jaylin Noel has added 186 yards on 8 catches.

Pressure allowed is about average (23% of dropbacks, 18th), but the 7.2% sack rate ranks 22nd. Four linemen have played every snap, with Ed Ingram and Wyatt Teller splitting right guard exactly in half. The run-blocking problem is still on the right side: 32 runs behind right guard and right tackle have averaged under 2 yards and about −0.5 EPA each, while runs up the middle average 4.6 yards.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Stroud turns pressure into sacks more often than average (30% vs. 26%), but FTN charged none of his 12 sacks to him: 8 came against a standard rush and 4 on extended plays, including one of each against Dallas. That still points mostly at protection, with his long time to throw as a contributing factor.

Houston still finishes its pressure better than almost anyone: 14 sacks on 159 dropbacks is an 8.8% sack rate, 2nd in the league, on 10.8 pressures per game (10th). Will Anderson leads with 12 pressures, 4.5 sacks, 11 QB hits and 7 tackles for loss; Danielle Hunter and Sheldon Rankins have 2 sacks each, and Jadeveon Clowney has 1.5 in part-time snaps. The run defense ranks 11th in EPA per rush.

The pass defense has slipped to 25th in EPA per dropback. Kamari Lassiter has allowed 20 catches on 27 targets for 251 yards (114.9 rating) and has 4 accepted penalties, tied for the most on the team. Derek Stingley Jr. has been better (11 of 24, 88.5 rating), while Reed Blankenship has allowed 17 of 23 for 241 yards and two touchdowns but has the unit's only interception.

The Texans allow a 101.3 passer rating in coverage (23rd; league 93.2) and 7.9 yards per target (20th), with 6 touchdowns and 1 interception on 141 targets. Opponents still throw at the safeties far more than usual (43% of targets, league 24%), and the safeties have allowed a 103.9 rating. The cornerbacks are at 103.4 on 52 targets (league cornerbacks 93.3).

Ka'imi Fairbairn is 7 of 8 on field goals with a long of 58 and perfect on 9 extra points. Kai Kroeger averages 49.1 yards per punt (43.5 net) with 6 inside the 20. Jaylin Noel (26.1 yards on 10 kickoff returns) and Woody Marks (24.3) handle most kickoffs. DVOA ranks the unit 28th, and Houston's 10 accepted special-teams penalties are the most in the league.

Indianapolis is 2–2 after a 30–13 win at Washington built on the run game (+0.28 EPA per rush) and the defense's best day of the season (−0.25 EPA per play). Over four games the Colts rank 3rd in EPA per rush but 30th passing, and the defense has climbed from 31st to 26th in EPA per play. They are also the league's least-penalized team at 4.0 accepted flags per game.
DVOA has Indianapolis 20th overall (−6.5%), up from 24th. The offense is 22nd and the defense 25th, with special teams (3rd) still the clear strength.

The Colts lean on play action more than most (31% of dropbacks, 4th; league 24%). Two-back looks are 17% of snaps and have produced +0.32 EPA per play, against −0.15 with one back, and even runs into seven-man boxes have been positive (+0.14 EPA on 52% of runs). On defense the blitz still backfires: five or more rushers have allowed +0.21 EPA per dropback on 31 plays against +0.09 with four, and Indianapolis blitzes on only 20% of dropbacks (league 31%).

Indianapolis uses presnap motion on 60% of plays (12th; league 58%), and the offense is better with it: −0.02 EPA per play with motion against −0.14 without, the 10th-largest gain. Motion runs have been the best part of it at +0.20 EPA per carry (2nd), and the passing game is poor either way but worse without motion (−0.38 EPA per pass play vs. −0.13 with it). On defense the Colts have struggled against runs with motion (+0.06 EPA per run, 30th) more than without (−0.06).

Week 4 was Daniel Jones's roughest passing game: 19 of 34 for 143 yards and an interception, 9.9% below expected completion rate by Next Gen Stats, with an average throw of 4.5 air yards. For the season he is at −0.21 EPA per dropback (32nd of 33 qualifiers) with 3 touchdowns and 4 interceptions, and his throws land 2.7 yards short of the sticks on average. FTN has charted 6 interception-worthy throws (league average 4.2), and play action hasn't helped (−0.25 EPA per dropback with it, −0.19 without).

Jonathan Taylor carries the load: 86 carries for 4.1 yards per carry, +0.06 EPA per carry and a 44% success rate. He is still running below Next Gen Stats' expectation (−0.31 yards per carry, 33rd of 46 qualifiers), so the efficiency comes from steady gains rather than creating extra yards. Seth McGowan has 3 broken tackles on just 12 carries, and the team's 7 broken tackles in four games rank 22nd per game (Pro Football Reference).

Josh Downs is still the best weapon: 28 targets (23% share), 37% of the team's air yards, +0.49 EPA per target and 1.5 yards of YAC over expected. Tyler Warren has 23 catches on 27 targets with two touchdowns, but his average target is just 2.2 yards downfield and he has three drops. Keenan Allen has 13 catches on 20 targets for −0.12 EPA per target, and Laquon Treadwell has added 123 yards on 9 catches.

The same five linemen have played nearly every snap (Bortolini, Goncalves and Travis all of them, Nelson 99% and Raimann 97%), and the line has yet to be flagged for an accepted penalty. They allow pressure on 20% of dropbacks (7th) and a 5.6% sack rate (15th). Every running lane except right guard has produced positive EPA, but contact still comes early: 2.0 yards before contact per carry ranks 26th (PFR).

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Jones is pressured less than average (20% of dropbacks vs. 23%) and converts pressure to sacks at about the league rate (28% vs. 26%). FTN charted his 8 sacks as 3 standard rushes, 3 blitzes and 1 extended play, plus the first one it has charged to him, against Washington.

The pass rush is still thin: 7.8 pressures per game ranks 20th and the 5.9% sack rate is 17th. DeForest Buckner leads with 7 pressures, 3 sacks and 7 QB hits, Adetomiwa Adebawore has 2 sacks in part-time work (32% of snaps), and Laiatu Latu has 6 pressures. The run defense is 28th in EPA per rush, though heavy boxes have stuffed opponents (−0.56 EPA per run on 12 runs).

Pass defense is 24th in EPA per dropback. Charvarius Ward has been the best of the group (5 of 16 for 87 yards, 50.8 rating), while Justin Walley (19 of 27 for 227 yards) and Sauce Gardner (12 of 20 for 235 yards, 117.7 rating) have given up the most. Safety A.J. Haulcy has allowed only 4 catches on 16 targets, but for 188 yards and two touchdowns.

The Colts allow 9.2 yards per target in coverage, still last in the league, and a 104.1 passer rating (27th; league 93.2), with 7 touchdowns and 1 interception on 139 targets. Linebackers have allowed 26 completions on 29 targets for 305 yards, and safeties have given up 4 touchdowns on 30 targets (125.1 rating). The cornerbacks are the steadiest group at 92.6 on 68 targets, now just under the league cornerback mark of 93.3.

Still a real strength. Spencer Shrader is 11 for 11 on field goals with a long of 58 (9 of 10 on extra points), Seth McGowan averages 29.5 yards on 11 kickoff returns, and Rigoberto Sanchez averages 51.7 yards per punt (46.2 net). DVOA ranks the unit 3rd.

Jacksonville is 3–1 after a 22–17 win at Cincinnati and still looks like one of the most complete teams in the league. It allows 13.3 points per game (2nd) with a +51 point differential, and ranks 4th in offensive EPA per play, 3rd in success rate and 7th in defensive EPA. Cincinnati gained 437 yards in Week 4, but two takeaways and +0.21 EPA per play on offense carried the win.
DVOA still ranks Jacksonville 2nd overall (40.1%), behind only San Francisco. The offense is 4th, the defense 3rd and special teams 18th.

Jacksonville uses empty sets more than most (9% of snaps, league 6%) and they keep working (+0.88 EPA per play on 19 plays), while its two-back looks (21%) average +0.27. It plays more tight ends than average (1.54 per snap, league 1.43). On defense it fields the fewest defensive backs in the league (4.15 per snap), and the blitz is still the weapon: five or more rushers have held offenses to −0.45 EPA per dropback on 41 plays, against +0.11 with four.

Jacksonville uses presnap motion on 61% of plays (10th; league 58%) and has been efficient either way: +0.18 EPA per play with motion and +0.19 without, both top-10 marks. The defense is where motion shows up. Without it opponents have managed −0.17 EPA per play (3rd), but with it they average +0.05 (23rd), the 4th-largest motion gain allowed in the league, and runs show the same gap (−0.29 EPA without vs. −0.02 with).

Trevor Lawrence stays efficient: +0.28 EPA per dropback (6th of 33 qualifiers), completions 6.8% above expectation by Next Gen Stats (4th), 8 touchdowns and 2 interceptions. He went 18 of 23 for 227 yards and a touchdown at Cincinnati, getting the ball out in 2.48 seconds. The blitz is still the weak spot: −0.10 EPA per dropback when blitzed against +0.43 when not.

Bhayshul Tuten remains the lead back: 60 carries at 4.6 yards per carry and 0.67 yards over Next Gen Stats' expectation (9th of 46 qualifiers). He does most of his work after contact (165 of his 277 yards in PFR charting), because the team averages only 1.9 yards before contact (28th). Chris Rodriguez Jr. is running close to expectation (−0.09). Jacksonville has 7 broken tackles in four games (22nd per game, PFR), 3 of them Tuten's.

Parker Washington still leads with 26 targets (26% share) and 44% of the team's air yards, turning them into 16 catches, 228 yards, two touchdowns and +0.42 EPA per target. Jakobi Meyers remains the most efficient: 13 catches on 15 targets, two touchdowns and +1.22 EPA per target. Brenton Strange has become a steady third option (14 of 18 for 167 yards, 3.7 yards of separation), while Brian Thomas Jr. has 9 catches on 14 targets with two drops.

Protection slipped in Week 4, when Cincinnati sacked Lawrence 4 times; the season sack rate is now 7.1% (21st) even though pressure stays below average (22% of dropbacks, 12th). Anton Harrison and Emmanuel Pregnon have played every snap, with Robert Hainsey, Ezra Cleveland and Cole Van Lanen at 90–96%. The run game wins outside and up the middle (left end 5.6 yards per carry, right end +0.37 EPA), while runs behind every guard and tackle spot have averaged negative EPA.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Lawrence now turns pressure into sacks more often than average (32% vs. 26%), up from 22% after Week 3. FTN charged none of his 8 sacks to him: 4 came against a standard rush, 2 against a blitz and 2 on extended plays.

10 sacks on 156 dropbacks is a 6.4% sack rate (13th), on 9.8 pressures per game (13th). Josh Hines-Allen leads with 8 pressures and 1.5 sacks, Travon Walker has 6 pressures and 1.5 sacks, and Dennis Gardeck adds 4 QB hits in part-time snaps. The run defense is 8th in EPA per rush.

8th in pass defense EPA, and opponents keep giving the ball away: FTN has charted 10 interception-worthy throws against Jacksonville, the most in the league (league average 4.2). Jourdan Lewis and Foyesade Oluokun have 2 interceptions each, and Jarrian Jones and Travis Hunter 1 each. Jones has been targeted most (31 times, 17 catches, 256 yards), and Montaric Brown remains the soft spot at a 131.1 passer rating allowed.

The Jaguars allow an 80.8 passer rating in coverage (5th; league 93.2), built on 3 touchdowns allowed (tied for fewest) and 6 interceptions (tied for most) on 149 targets. The catch is still yardage, at 8.7 yards per target (29th). Cornerbacks, counting Travis Hunter, see 54% of targets and have allowed a 72.7 rating with four of the six interceptions, while the safeties have allowed 120.9 on 23 targets.

Cam Little is 7 of 9 on field goals with a long of 55 and perfect on 11 extra points. Logan Cooke averages 48.4 yards per punt (43.4 net) with 5 inside the 20. Josh Cameron and Ameer Abdullah handle kickoffs at 25.9 and 27.7 yards per return. DVOA ranks the unit 18th.

4–0 with a +41 point differential after a 30–27 win in Las Vegas. Kansas City ranks 5th in offensive EPA per play, 1st in EPA per rush and 6th in success rate. The defense slipped to 9th in EPA per play after allowing 437 yards to the Raiders, but still allows 19.3 points per game (6th).
