DVOA has Kansas City 3rd overall, with the 5th-ranked offense and the 10th-ranked defense. Special teams moved up from 20th to 16th.

Kansas City still leads the league in play action (36% of dropbacks, league 24%) and screens (18%, league 8%). Two-back looks (19% of snaps) are at +0.17 EPA per play, a bit better than one-back sets (+0.13). On defense the four-man rush holds offenses to −0.04 EPA per dropback (league +0.10), while blitzes with five or more have been hit for +0.09 on 45 plays.

Kansas City motions on 59% of plays (14th; league 58%) and is one of the few offenses that is better without it: +0.32 EPA per play without motion (3rd) against +0.08 with it. The gap is all in the run game, where runs without motion average 8.0 yards and +0.41 EPA (both 1st) and runs after motion 4.0 yards and −0.09. On defense, only three teams have faced motion more often (68% of plays), and passes after motion have hurt (+0.11 EPA per dropback against −0.28 without).

Patrick Mahomes is still playing fast and short: 2.70 seconds to throw (4th-fastest of 33 qualifiers), 7.1 intended air yards and tight-window throws on 8.6% of attempts (qualifier average 15.0%). He is at +0.21 EPA per dropback (10th), with 9 touchdowns, 2 interceptions and a 106.2 passer rating, completing 1.5% below Next Gen Stats' expectation. Play action (+0.32 EPA per dropback against +0.14) and the blitz (+0.42 when blitzed) both help him.

Kenneth Walker III is still the best runner in the league by Next Gen Stats: 87 carries for 537 yards, 6.2 yards per carry and 2.52 yards over expected per carry, first of 46 qualifiers. He leads the league with 14 broken tackles (12 on runs) per Pro Football Reference and has 267 yards after contact. Kansas City remains 1st in broken tackles per game (5.0).

Travis Kelce is the most efficient regular target: 16 catches on 22 targets for 246 yards, 2 touchdowns, +0.74 EPA per target and 3.5 yards of YAC over expected. Tyquan Thornton is the deep threat (17.4-yard average depth, 219 yards, 2 touchdowns, +1.27 EPA per target). Rashee Rice (13 of 17, 190 yards) gets 4.1 yards of separation. Xavier Worthy is tied with Kelce for the team lead in targets (22) but is at 6.0 yards per target and −0.15 EPA per target.

Mahomes is pressured on 22% of dropbacks (11th) and sacked on 4.2% (7th). Creed Humphrey, Trey Smith, Kahlil Benson and Jaylon Moore have played nearly every snap, with Kingsley Suamataia (77%) and Mike Caliendo (25%) splitting the fifth spot. Kansas City now averages 2.7 yards before contact per carry (10th, up from 24th). Outside runs carry the ground game: left end runs average 10.8 yards and +0.65 EPA, while the 42 runs up the middle average 3.2 yards at −0.15 EPA.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Mahomes turns pressure into sacks less often than most (19% vs. 26% league; 9th-lowest of 36). FTN charted 4 of his 6 sacks as a standard rush winning; the two in Week 4 were an extended play and a blitz.

The pass rush is the weak spot: only 4 sacks and a 2.5% sack rate, 31st. George Karlaftis III leads with 13 pressures and 10 QB hits but still has no sacks. R Mason Thomas has 8 pressures and a sack. As a unit Kansas City averages 9.8 pressure credits per game (13th; league 9.3), and the run defense ranks 9th.

9th in pass defense EPA. L'Jarius Sneed is still targeted most (33) and has allowed 26 catches for 247 yards. Mansoor Delane has allowed 12 of 18 for 117 yards with an interception and 3 passes defensed, and Nohl Williams has 4 passes defensed with a 67.5 rating allowed. Kristian Fulton has allowed 13 yards on 7 targets with an interception.

Kansas City has allowed an 80.3 passer rating in coverage (4th; league 93.2) and 6.6 yards per target (5th), though opponents complete 64% of their throws (23rd). The linebackers have been hardest to throw on (70.4 rating), led by Drue Tranquill (4 of 11 for 45 yards). The soft spots are Sneed (108.0) and the safeties Jaden Hicks (108.5) and Alohi Gilman (110.4).

Harrison Butker is 7 of 9 on field goals with a long of 46 and 13 of 13 on extra points. Matt Araiza averages 52.3 yards per punt (47.3 net) with 9 of 12 inside the 20. Emmett Johnson (28.5), Brashard Smith (26.6) and Nikko Remigio (25.0) share kickoff returns. DVOA ranks the unit 16th.

The Rams are 2–2 but play like a top-ten team. They rank 3rd in defensive EPA per play and 2nd against the pass, and won 24–20 at Philadelphia in Week 4 while outgaining the Eagles 416 to 172. The offense is 11th in EPA per play. Two giveaways in every game (8 total against 3 takeaways) are why the record lags.
DVOA ranks the Rams 7th (18.0%), with the 7th-ranked offense and 4th-ranked defense. Special teams are still last at −14.5%.

One of the heaviest offenses: 1.7 tight ends per snap (5th most) and the 4th-fewest backs. It sees eight-man boxes on 15% of runs (league 9%), and those runs average −0.43 EPA; two-back looks (−0.35) and empty sets (−0.39) have both lost value. The defense plays the 2nd-most defensive backs and is far better sending extra rushers: −0.42 EPA per dropback with five or more against −0.05 with four.

The Rams use motion on 63% of plays (8th) and are worse with it: −0.06 EPA per play with motion against +0.17 without, the 4th-largest drop in the league. On passes the gap is −0.08 against +0.21. The defense flips the pattern: offenses gain 0.40 EPA per play from motion against Los Angeles (2nd most), because without it the Rams allow −0.37, the best mark in the league.

Matthew Stafford is 18th of 33 qualifiers at +0.05 EPA per dropback, with 6 touchdowns and 6 interceptions after going 0 and 2 at Philadelphia. He still pushes the ball (9.6-yard average depth of target) and completes 1.2 points above expectation. FTN has charted 10 interception-worthy throws for the offense, the most in the league (average 4.2). Blitzes remain his problem: −0.33 EPA per dropback when opponents send extra rushers against +0.19 when they don't.

Kyren Williams is running well: 294 yards at 5.4 per carry, +1.06 yards over Next Gen Stats' expectation (8th of 46 qualifiers) and +0.05 EPA per carry, plus 21 catches for 173 yards. Blake Corum adds 4.9 per carry (+0.26 over expected). The backs get about 3 yards before contact (2nd), though broken tackles are scarce: 8 as a team (18th per game), 5 of them by Williams.

Davante Adams is the downfield target: 22 catches for 390 yards and 2 touchdowns on 38 targets, a 15.7-yard average depth of target, 41% of the air yards and +0.39 EPA per target. Puka Nacua has 199 yards on 14 catches with 3.0 yards after the catch above expectation, and Tyler Higbee (15 of 19, 141 yards) has turned positive. FTN has charged the offense with 9 drops, 2nd most, 2 each by Adams, Terrance Ferguson and Blake Corum.

One of the best lines in football. Alaric Jackson, Steve Avila, Coleman Shelton and Warren McClendon have played every snap and Kevin Dotson 99%. Pressure comes on 18% of dropbacks (2nd lowest), the sack rate is 3.5% (4th), and backs get 3.0 yards before contact (2nd). Runs behind right guard (−0.54 EPA on 17 carries) are still the leak, while 34 runs up the middle average 5.8 yards.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, a measure that mostly reflects the QB) plus FTN's charting of each sack. There have been six, and FTN charged none to Stafford. Three came when a standard rush won, two against blitzes and one on an extended play, and his 20% pressure-to-sack rate is below the 26% league average.

The pass rush is finishing more: 7 sacks after 3 through Week 3, though volume is still low (7.8 pressures per game, 20th; 5.1% sack rate, 21st). Byron Young leads with 3.5 sacks, 11 pressures, 6 QB hits and a forced fumble, and Omar Speights has 2 sacks. The run defense has climbed to 10th in EPA per rush from 23rd a week ago.

2nd in EPA per dropback allowed. Trent McDuffie has allowed 7 catches for 42 yards on 21 targets (a 23 passer rating) with 7 passes defensed and an interception, and Quentin Lake has 7 passes defensed, an interception and a forced fumble on 24 targets (65 rating). Josh Wallace (28 rating) has an interception. Jaylen Watson (2 touchdowns, 135 rating) and Kamren Kinchens (2 touchdowns on 5 targets) are the soft spots.

PFR's charting agrees. The Rams allow a 78.4 passer rating (3rd; league 93.2) and 5.0 yards per target (1st): 68 of 122 for 615 yards, 7 touchdowns and 3 interceptions. Cornerbacks are the strength at a 62.7 rating with 2 interceptions (3rd among cornerback groups). Safeties see 35% of the targets (2nd most; league 24%) and allow a 96.6 rating.
Last in special teams DVOA. Harrison Mevis is 5 of 7 on field goals with a long of 48, Ethan Evans nets 37.9 yards per punt, and Xavier Smith averages 20.6 yards per kickoff return.

0–4 with a −39 point differential after a 23–30 loss at Seattle in which the Chargers turned it over 4 times. The offense is last in EPA per play, 29th passing and 26th rushing, and scores 16.8 points per game (29th). The defense has climbed to 12th in EPA per play, with a 7th-ranked sack rate.
DVOA ranks the Chargers 31st. The offense is now last (32nd), the defense 20th and special teams 29th.

The Chargers still run the heaviest backfield in the league: two or more backs on 39% of snaps (1st; league 20%), and they go empty on 10% (3rd; league 6%). None of it has worked: −0.19 EPA per play with two backs, −0.16 with one and −0.02 from empty. They play the second-fewest tight ends (1.14 per snap). On defense, extra rushers have been the answer: −0.30 EPA per dropback with five or more on 34 plays, against +0.18 with four.

Los Angeles motions on 72% of plays (3rd; league 58%), and nobody has gotten less out of it: −0.25 EPA per play after motion (32nd) against +0.06 without. Passes after motion are at −0.25 EPA per dropback with a 34% success rate (31st). On defense the Chargers handle motion well (−0.08 EPA per play, 3rd) but allow +0.12 when offenses line up still.

Justin Herbert is at −0.15 EPA per dropback (29th of 33 qualifiers), completing 3.6% below Next Gen Stats' expectation, with 4 touchdowns, 6 interceptions and a 70.6 passer rating. FTN has charted 9 interception-worthy throws, 2nd-most in the league (league average 4.2). Play action is the one thing working (+0.12 EPA per dropback against −0.26), and he is at −0.32 when blitzed.

Omarion Hampton has 9 broken tackles on runs (tied for 3rd in the league in total broken tackles, Pro Football Reference) but is averaging 4.0 yards per carry and −0.22 EPA per carry. He is now 0.07 yards below Next Gen Stats' expectation (23rd of 46, up from 31st). Keaton Mitchell runs for 4.6 yards per carry and has caught 9 of 10 targets. The Chargers are 2nd in broken tackles per game (4.8).

Tre Harris has become the lead receiver: 13 catches on 21 targets for 209 yards, +0.28 EPA per target and 3.4 yards of separation. Ladd McConkey is still the most efficient (12 of 17, 183 yards, +0.63 EPA per target) but was held without a catch in Week 4. Quentin Johnston has caught 7 of 19 with 2 drops, and tight end Oronde Gadsden II is at −0.39 EPA on 15 targets.

The line is still the biggest problem. Herbert is pressured on 30% of dropbacks (31st) and sacked on 8.3% (26th). Offensive linemen have drawn 18 accepted penalties, the most of any line, led by Joe Alt (6, including 4 false starts); Alt played 83% of snaps, with Travis Burke filling in. The 29 runs up the middle have cost −0.35 EPA each; only left guard (+0.41 on 10) and right tackle runs have been positive.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Week 4 pointed at Herbert for the first time: FTN charged all 4 of his sacks at Seattle to him, after charging him with none of the first 8. For the season he converts pressure to sacks at 29% (league 26%), and 4 of his 12 sacks came against a blitz.

Khalil Mack leads with 10 pressures, 3 sacks and 5 tackles for loss, and Tuli Tuipulotu has 8 pressures, 2 sacks and 7 QB hits. As a unit the Chargers average 9.8 pressure credits per game (13th) and rank 7th in sack rate with 10 sacks. The run defense ranks 15th.

19th in pass defense EPA. Cam Hart has allowed 167 yards on 16 targets but has an interception and 4 passes defensed, and Genesis Smith still has 2 interceptions. Offenses are picking on the linebackers: Del'Shawn Phillips has allowed 9 of 9 (131.0 rating) and Daiyan Henley 8 of 11 for 97 yards.

The Chargers have allowed a 93.6 passer rating in coverage (20th; league 93.2), and opponents complete 66% of their throws (28th) for 8.0 yards per target (22nd). The cornerbacks give up the most per throw (9.7 yards per target), and the linebackers have allowed 22 of 28 for a 106.1 rating. Tony Jefferson (128.6) is the most-beaten safety.

Cameron Dicker is 6 of 8 on field goals with a long of 40 and 7 of 7 on extra points. J.K. Scott averages 48.1 yards per punt (43.1 net) with 4 inside the 20. Keaton Mitchell returns kickoffs at 24.9 yards. DVOA still ranks the unit 29th.

3–1 with a +31 point differential after a 27–30 home loss to Kansas City, the Raiders' first game without a takeaway (9 on the season, against 6 giveaways). Las Vegas ranks 4th in defensive EPA per play, 5th against the pass, 7th against the run and 5th in sack rate. The offense is 14th in EPA per play: 11th passing, but 29th rushing.
DVOA slid Las Vegas from 9th to 12th, with the 14th-ranked offense, the 11th-ranked defense and special teams at 10th.

Las Vegas is still a heavy team: two or more backs on 34% of snaps (4th; league 20%) and the fewest receivers on the field (1.9 per snap; league 2.4), with 1.7 tight ends (4th). Two-back looks (+0.07 EPA per play) and empty sets (+0.35 on 16 plays) have beaten one-back sets (−0.06). The defense rarely blitzes (25% of dropbacks, 23rd), but five or more rushers have held offenses to −0.32 EPA per dropback on 37 plays.

Las Vegas motions on 66% of plays (6th; league 58%). It lifts the passing game (+0.27 EPA per dropback after motion, 5th, against −0.03 without) but sinks the run game (−0.34 EPA per carry after motion, 32nd). The defense is the league's best against motion: it has faced it more than anyone (71% of plays) and allows −0.21 EPA per play on those snaps (1st), against +0.17 without.

Kirk Cousins has been efficient: +0.17 EPA per dropback (12th of 33 qualifiers), 11 touchdowns, 4 interceptions, a 99.5 passer rating and 2.6% above Next Gen Stats' completion expectation. He threw 52 passes against Kansas City. He still rarely leaves the pocket (11% of dropbacks, 3rd-lowest; league 20%), and play action remains a big lever (+0.39 EPA per dropback against +0.09).

Ashton Jeanty is still stuck: 78 carries at 3.4 yards per carry, −0.29 EPA per carry and a 32% success rate, 0.11 yards below Next Gen Stats' expectation (27th of 46). He has 5 broken tackles on runs (Pro Football Reference), and adds 19 catches for 165 yards and 2 touchdowns, though with 3 drops. Mike Washington Jr. averages 5.0 yards per carry.

Targets are spread evenly: Jeanty, Michael Mayer and Brock Bowers have 24 each and Tre Tucker 23. Bowers has been the most productive (16 catches, 202 yards, 2 touchdowns, +0.57 EPA per target). Tucker is the deep threat (14.9-yard average depth, 30% of the air yards, 233 yards). Mayer has caught 20 of 24, and Cody White has 3 touchdowns on 10 targets.

Pass protection slipped: Cousins has been pressured on 26% of dropbacks (28th, down from 9th), though the 3.4% sack rate is 3rd and he wasn't sacked in Week 4. Jackson Powers-Johnson (69%) and Caleb Rogers (31%) now share one guard spot; the other four linemen have played every snap. The run blocking is the bigger issue: 1.4 yards before contact per carry (32nd), every run direction is negative, and the 41 runs up the middle average 3.3 yards at −0.19 EPA.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Cousins rarely lets pressure become a sack (13% vs. 26% league, 3rd-lowest of 36). FTN charted his 5 sacks as 2 standard rushes, 2 charged to him and 1 extended play, and none came in Weeks 1 or 4.

Las Vegas averages 14.0 pressure credits per game, 2nd in the league (league 9.3). Maxx Crosby leads with 18 pressures and 11 QB hits, now with 2 sacks. Malcolm Koonce (2.5), Kwity Paye (2) and Nakobe Dean (1.5) have also finished, for 12 sacks and a 5th-ranked sack rate. The run defense ranks 7th, and runs into eight-man boxes have been stuffed at −0.96 EPA per carry on 7 plays.

5th in pass defense EPA. Hezekiah Masses has 3 interceptions and 6 passes defensed and has allowed a 42.9 passer rating on 20 targets. Eric Stokes is the most-targeted defender (22 targets, 87.5 rating). Linebacker Nakobe Dean has allowed 12 catches on 13 targets.

Las Vegas has allowed an 88.9 passer rating in coverage (12th, down from 8th; league 93.2). The cornerbacks carry it: a 60.3 rating and 47% completions on 64 targets. The safeties are the soft spot at a 127.5 rating, 11.0 yards per target and 4 of the 7 touchdowns, with Isaiah Pola-Mao (2 touchdowns on 7 targets) and Jeremy Chinn (7 of 8) the most beaten.

Matt Gay is 10 for 10 on field goals with a long of 59 and 9 of 9 on extra points. AJ Cole averages 50.4 yards per punt (45.4 net) with 7 inside the 20. Dylan Laube averages 33.4 yards per kickoff return and Malik Benson 13.6 per punt return. DVOA ranks the unit 10th.

Miami is 0–4 after a 15–10 loss at Minnesota. The offense ranks 30th in EPA per play, 31st in success rate and last in scoring (11.5 points per game). The defense is 28th in EPA per play and 30th against the pass, but held Minnesota to 15 points. The −55 point differential is the league's worst by 16 points.
DVOA still has Miami 32nd overall, the only team below −40%. The offense is 30th, the defense 28th and special teams 31st.

Miami plays the fewest tight ends in the league (1.1 on the field on average) and more backs than most (6th). Two-back looks take 29% of snaps (league 20%) and lose −0.18 EPA per play; one-back sets aren't much better (−0.15). On defense, the rush count hasn't mattered: four rushers allow +0.25 EPA per dropback and five or more allow +0.47.

Miami motions more than any team, on 80% of snaps (league 58%), and it hasn't worked. Plays with motion average −0.18 EPA (30th) and a 31% success rate (last), against +0.03 and 49% without. Passes after motion average 5.0 yards against 9.3 without. On defense, opponents' passes after motion have gained +0.38 EPA per play, 31st.

Malik Willis ranks 27th of 33 qualified quarterbacks in EPA per dropback (−0.11), with one touchdown and two interceptions. Week 4 was his worst passing game: 9 of 17 for 85 yards, 12 points below Next Gen Stats' expected completion rate. He still throws into tight windows on 20% of attempts (5th highest). Blitzes hurt most (−0.34 EPA per dropback blitzed, +0.01 not), and play action has helped (+0.07 vs. −0.18).

The run game ranks 27th in EPA per carry, though Week 4 was its best game (+0.18). Ollie Gordon II has overtaken De'Von Achane: 148 yards on 29 carries (5.1 per carry), 0.5 over Next Gen Stats' expectation (10th of 46) and four broken tackles on runs (Pro Football Reference charting), but only a 24% success rate. Achane averages 3.7, 0.3 below expectation (31st).

Malik Washington draws 27% of targets and 31% of air yards, and his EPA per target has improved to about break-even (−0.05). Chris Bell runs the deepest routes of any NGS-qualified receiver (18.0-yard average depth of target) and adds 3.8 yards of YAC over expectation (4th), but has 5 catches on 13 targets. Caleb Douglas has 113 yards on 10 targets; Kevin Coleman Jr. has 6 yards on 10.

The same five linemen have played every snap. Miami allows pressure on 27% of dropbacks (29th) and a sack on 8.7% (27th). Runs to the right have been worst: right guard runs average 3.3 yards and right tackle runs lose yardage. The line has 12 accepted penalties, 7 for holding, tied for 5th most among lines.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. This one leans toward the quarterback. FTN charged four of Willis's 11 sacks to him and two more came on extended plays outside the pocket. His pressure-to-sack rate (31% vs. 26%) is above average. Both Week 4 sacks were on the line, one against a standard rush and one on a blitz.

The first four sacks of the season all came in Week 4 at Minnesota: two from Zach Sieler, one each from Joshua Uche and Chop Robinson. Volume is still low at 6.8 pressures per game (25th; league 9.3), with Robinson leading at nine. The run defense is a strength at 6th in EPA per rush, and Sieler has five tackles for loss.

The pass defense is 30th in EPA per dropback. Chris Johnson has allowed three touchdowns on 19 targets (131.8 rating), Michael Taaffe 178 yards on 14 targets despite an interception, and linebacker Willie Gay Jr. all seven targets for 103 yards.

Miami allows a 112.8 passer rating in coverage (31st; league 93.2) and a 72.7% completion rate, with nine touchdowns on 121 targets. Cornerbacks (124.1) and linebackers (115.6) both rank 31st among their groups, and linebackers see 39% of targets (league 27%), with Jordyn Brooks allowing 12 of 16. The three interceptions came from Jacob Rodriguez, Taaffe and Dante Trader.

Special teams rank 31st in DVOA. Riley Patterson is 6 of 8 on field goals with a long of 41. Jaylen Wright averages 28.2 yards on 10 kick returns. Bradley Pinion nets 38.1 yards per punt on 15 punts, five inside the 20.

4–0, and the whole thing rests on the defense. Minnesota is 1st in defensive EPA per play, 1st in success rate, 1st in sack rate and 1st in points allowed at 12.75 a game. The offense is 27th in EPA per play and last in the league in success rate at 33.1%, so the margins stay thin: 21.5 points a game and four wins by 17, 6, 7 and 5. A +5 turnover margin and 289 yards allowed a game are doing the work of an offense.
DVOA agrees on the shape and ranks it 10th overall at +11.2%: the 2nd-ranked defense (−22.3%) and the No. 1 special teams (+12.3%) covering for the 31st-ranked offense (−23.4%).

The offense leans on extra backs more than most, two or more on 28% of snaps against a 20% league rate, and those looks are the least bad (0.00 EPA against −0.13 for one-back sets, −0.37 for the eight empty snaps). Play action is the one real lever, +0.34 EPA per dropback against −0.22 without it, used on 27% of dropbacks. The defense is the most aggressive in football by a distance: five or more rushers on 72.6% of dropbacks against a 31% league rate, and it holds offenses to about −0.16 EPA per dropback whether it sends four or more, which is why there is no obvious way to make it stop.

Motion barely helps the offense: −0.08 EPA per play with it against −0.13 without, a +0.05 gain that ranks 13th, on a 56.7% rate. The number that matters is on the other side. Minnesota is close to unplayable when the offense stands still — −0.31 EPA per play, 2nd in the league, and 3.8 yards per pass play, the best mark in football — but only −0.07 against motion, a +0.24 gap that ranks 30th. It is the one repeatable way anyone has moved the ball on this defense, and opponents have used it less than you would expect, motioning on 53.6% of snaps against the Vikings, 27th.

Kyler Murray has the job and has not solved it: −0.16 EPA per dropback over 84 dropbacks (30th among qualified passers) with one touchdown and two interceptions. Week 4 against Miami was his cleanest game, 27 of 37 for 247 yards, no turnovers and completions 3.9 points above expectation, but it came on a 4.9-yard average target depth and an average throw 4.3 yards short of the sticks. Carson Wentz's 47 dropbacks still rate better (+0.08, three touchdowns, no interceptions) despite completions 7.8 points below expectation, and he was sacked on 12.8% of them.

Aaron Jones is the entire run game, 72 carries against 15 for Jordan Mason and six for Demond Claiborne, and he is at 4.1 yards per carry with a 35% success rate and −0.43 yards per carry against Next Gen Stats' expectation. What stands out is contact: Minnesota has five broken tackles in four games, 1.25 a game (27th), and exactly one of them is Jones's, on 81 touches (Pro Football Reference charting). The blocking is unremarkable rather than bad at 2.39 yards before contact (17th), so this is a yards-after-contact problem.

T.J. Hockenson is now the focal point and the volume leader: 22 catches on 26 targets for 195 yards, +0.63 EPA per target and 3.3 yards of separation, though he is 106th of 111 qualified receivers in YAC above expectation, so it is all catches and no extra. Justin Jefferson has not added a target since Week 3 and has played 47% of the snaps; his 13 catches for 179 yards and two touchdowns at +0.93 EPA per target remain the best efficiency on the roster and the clearest thing the offense is missing. Jordan Addison has the deep role (37% of the air yards, a 13.8-yard average depth) and has caught 11 of 22 for −0.10 EPA per target.

Blake Brandel, Will Fries and Brian O'Neill have played all 254 snaps, with Christian Darrisaw at 86% and Donovan Jackson at 72%. Pressure allowed is middling at 23.5% (19th), but far too much of it ends on the ground: 13 sacks on 131 dropbacks, a 9.9% rate that ranks 31st. On the ground only right end (+0.27 on seven carries) and right tackle (+0.04 on 11) are positive, and the two most-used lanes, right guard (23 carries, 3.3 yards) and the middle (20, 2.7), are where the offense keeps going anyway.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. It still splits by quarterback. Wentz was pressured on only 19% of dropbacks but 6 of his 9 pressures became sacks, a 67% rate that points squarely at protection; Murray is at 32% on heavier pressure. The charting agrees: FTN charged just one of the 13 sacks to a quarterback, six were standard four-man rushes beaten — including three of the four Miami got in Week 4 — and four were extended plays.

The best pass rush in football, by margin rather than by inches: 16.0 pressures per game against a 9.3 league average, 16 sacks and a 10.5% sack rate, both 1st. Dallas Turner has 22 pressures, 14 QB hits, 5.5 sacks and two forced fumbles; Andrew Van Ginkel has three sacks, an interception and a 2.8 passer rating allowed in coverage; Blake Cashman adds nine pressures and 2.5 sacks from linebacker; Kyle Van Noy has six tackles for loss on 32% of snaps. The run defense is 5th in EPA per rush, so there is no soft side to go at.

1st in pass defense EPA, and not only because of the rush. Isaiah Rodgers has allowed 7 of 19 for a 36.1 rating with an interception, James Pierre 5 of 12 for 19.4 with another, and Byron Murphy has held up on the heaviest volume at 18 of 26 for 231 yards (80.8) with a third interception. Safety is the one leak: Theo Jackson has allowed all three of his targets for 98 yards and two touchdowns (158.3), and Josh Metellus sits at 99.8 on 22 targets, the most of any defender here.

Minnesota has allowed a 72.6 passer rating in coverage, 2nd in the league, with the lowest completion rate in football at 55.3%, the fewest touchdowns (three) and four interceptions. The cornerbacks are the best group in the league at 53.0 on 57 targets with no touchdowns allowed and three interceptions, and the linebackers are 3rd at 59.1. All three touchdowns have come against the safeties, who sit 23rd at 114.6, two of them on Theo Jackson's three targets — so the only way through this coverage so far has been over the top of the safeties.

Will Reichard is 12 for 12 on field goals with a long of 56 and 6 for 6 on extra points, which is most of why Minnesota is 1st in special teams DVOA. Myles Price averages 30.2 yards per kickoff return and 20.1 per punt return. Two punters are splitting the work, Brett Thorson (10 punts, a 41.1-yard net, five inside the 20) and Johnny Hekker (12, 38.6, two inside the 20). The team is also the 5th-least-penalized in the league at 6.5 flags a game, with one defensive back penalty all season, tied for the fewest of any team.

The offense finally showed up in a 29–26 win at Buffalo, its best game by EPA per play (+0.18) and yardage (407), and the climb from 28th to 23rd in offensive EPA per play shows it. The defense still carries the team: 13th in EPA per play, 6th against the pass and 6th in points allowed (19.3 per game). The gap is turnovers, with 10 giveaways against 5 takeaways, and a run defense that ranks 30th.
DVOA has New England 26th overall at 2–2. The offense moved up from last to 26th after the Buffalo win, the defense is 7th, and special teams are 21st.

New England plays two or more backs on 28% of snaps (league 20%), and those looks keep failing at −0.31 EPA per play, against +0.06 in one-back sets. It uses fewer tight ends than most (26th). On defense, sending five or more rushers is still the better call (−0.13 EPA per dropback, against +0.01 with four), but runs into an eight-man box have gained +0.22 EPA per carry.

New England motions at about the league rate (55% of snaps, 20th; league 58%) and has been worse with it on both passes and runs. The run game is the problem: runs after motion average 2.5 yards, last in the league, against 4.2 without. On defense the pattern flips, with runs after motion held to −0.01 EPA against +0.14 without.

Drake Maye had his best game in Buffalo: 22 of 37 for 269 yards, three touchdowns and a 97.7 passer rating. For the season he ranks 21st of 33 qualified quarterbacks in EPA per dropback (+0.01), and his seven interceptions still lead the league. He holds the ball 3.04 seconds on average (6th longest), and play action has cost him (−0.16 EPA per dropback with it, +0.08 without).

Both backs are at or above Next Gen Stats' expected yardage, but neither produces positive EPA: Rhamondre Stevenson averages 3.7 yards on 44 carries (−0.06 EPA) and TreVeyon Henderson 3.7 on 38 (−0.15, 32% success rate). Henderson's edge over expectation has shrunk to 0.2 yards per carry. Through Week 4 no Patriots back has broken a tackle on a run (Pro Football Reference charting), and the team's 0.75 broken tackles per game rank 31st.

Mack Hollins and Romeo Doubs share the lead with 20 targets each. Hollins has been the more efficient (15 catches, 209 yards, +0.64 EPA per target); Doubs has the two touchdowns and gets 3.6 yards of separation on a 16-yard average depth of target, second only to Isaac TeSlaa among NGS-qualified receivers with a 14+ yard depth. DeMario Douglas has been held to 82 yards on 17 targets.

Will Campbell and Alijah Vera-Tucker have played every snap and Jared Wilson and Morgan Moses most of them, while five others have rotated through the remaining spot. The sack rate has improved to 6.8% (20th, from 29th) and Maye was sacked once in Buffalo, but pressure still comes on 25% of dropbacks (26th). Runs behind right guard average 2.6 yards at −0.33 EPA, and Campbell has four of the line's eight accepted penalties.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. This still points mostly at the line. Maye's pressure-to-sack rate (28% vs. 26%) is now close to average. FTN charged one of his 10 sacks to him, the lone sack in Week 4; six of the others came against a standard rush of four or fewer.

The pass rush is middle of the pack: 8.0 pressures per game (19th; league 9.3) and a sack rate that ranks 19th. Elijah Ponder leads with 2.5 sacks, six QB hits and four tackles for loss, Gabe Jacas has 1.5 sacks and an interception, and Christian Barmore adds a sack and a forced fumble. Run defense remains the problem at 30th in EPA per rush.

The pass defense ranks 6th in EPA per dropback. Christian Gonzalez has allowed 8 catches for 43 yards on 18 targets (51.6 rating), and Marcus Jones has an interception and four passes defensed on 20 targets. Craig Woodson's interception in Buffalo dropped his rating allowed from above 140 to 63.0; Kevin Byard is still at 140.6, and Charles Woods has allowed 156 yards on 14 targets.

New England allows a 91.2 passer rating in coverage (17th; league 93.2) and 7.3 yards per target (11th). The cornerbacks are 8th best among cornerback groups at 83.5 on 71 targets. Safeties improved from 147.2 to 109.7 (21st) after Woodson's interception, and linebackers are at 108.8 (26th), with Christian Elliss allowing 13 of 18 for 157 yards.

Andy Borregales is 5 of 7 on field goals with a long of 50 and 6 for 6 on extra points. Mitch Wishnowsky averages 48.3 yards gross and 40.7 net on 14 punts, with six inside the 20. Kyle Williams averages 24.8 yards on 11 kick returns. Special teams rank 21st in DVOA.

The defense has become the story of a 1–3 start. New Orleans now allows 32.0 points per game, most in the league, and ranks 30th in defensive EPA per play, 31st in success rate allowed and 32nd against the run. The 45–24 home loss to Atlanta (+0.42 EPA per play allowed, 422 yards) was the low point. The offense is middle of the pack, 15th in EPA per play and 10th in points per game, and eight giveaways against three takeaways have not helped.
DVOA agrees and has slid further: New Orleans is 30th overall (from 28th), with the defense 31st, the offense 21st and special teams 19th.

A spread offense with 2.65 receivers per snap (5th most) and few tight ends (23rd), and it sees light boxes on 67% of runs (league 45%) without taking advantage (−0.15 EPA per run). The defense keeps more linemen on the field than any team and the fewest linebackers. Blitzing keeps backfiring: sending five or more allows +0.32 EPA per dropback, against +0.13 with four rushers and a league rate of 0.00 when blitzing.

Motion hasn't helped either side of the ball. New Orleans motions on 59% of plays (13th; league 58%) and is slightly worse with it (−0.03 EPA per play) than without (+0.02), mostly because runs after motion fall to −0.15 EPA. The defense is hurt badly by it: runs after motion gain 5.5 yards with a 57% success rate and +0.23 EPA, all last in the league, compared with −0.04 EPA when the offense stays still.

Tyler Shough has been accurate but not efficient: completions 3.1 points above expectation (Next Gen Stats), 9 touchdowns, 3 interceptions and a 95.7 passer rating, yet only +0.03 EPA per dropback (20th of 33). The blitz is the biggest drag (−0.19 EPA per dropback when opponents send extra rushers, +0.12 when they don't). Play action works (+0.20 vs. −0.02) but New Orleans uses it on 18% of dropbacks, 29th. Against Atlanta he threw deeper than usual (10.2-yard average intended air yards) and went 30 of 48 for 286 yards.

Nobody has gotten the run game going. Travis Etienne leads with 4.3 yards per carry but is half a yard below Next Gen Stats' expectation, Alvin Kamara is at 3.0 yards per carry and 0.9 below expectation (44th of 46 qualifiers), and Kendre Miller has 53 yards on 19 carries (−0.40 EPA per carry). Through Week 3 the backs gained 2.3 yards before contact per carry (20th), while New Orleans broke 4.0 tackles per game (5th), led by Etienne (4) and tight end Juwan Johnson (3).

Chris Olave remains the focal point, with 28% of the targets and 45% of the air yards, and has turned that into 35 catches for 491 yards and +0.73 EPA per target. Juwan Johnson is the best efficiency target: 21 catches on 27 targets, 3 touchdowns, 3.8 yards of separation and 1.4 yards after the catch above expectation. Devaughn Vele (21 catches, 226 yards, 2 touchdowns) is close behind, and Noah Fant has 3 touchdowns on 8 catches. Bryce Lance gets the deep shots (16.0-yard average depth of target) but has caught 5 of 13.

Pass protection holds up until the sack. Through Week 3 New Orleans allowed pressure on 20% of dropbacks (6th lowest), and the 6.1% sack rate ranks 18th. Four linemen (Fuaga, Edwards, McCoy and Ruiz) have played every snap, with Kelvin Banks and Asim Richards splitting left tackle. Runs up the middle work (3.7 yards per carry, +0.20 EPA, 53% success on 40 carries); runs behind right tackle have one success in 12 tries.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, a measure that mostly reflects the QB) plus FTN's charting of each sack. It leans toward the quarterback and the blitz pickup. Through Week 3 Shough was pressured less than average but turned 10 of his 29 pressures into sacks (34% vs. 26%). Of the 12 sacks, FTN put 5 on a standard rush, 4 on blitzes, 2 on Shough and 1 on an extended play; Atlanta's two in Week 4 came on a six-man blitz and a four-man rush on fourth down.

The run defense is last in EPA per rush allowed (+0.11), and the pass rush is middling: 9.7 pressures per game through Week 3 (16th) and a 5.9% sack rate (18th). Chase Young has been the bright spot with 3.5 sacks, 5 QB hits and 3 tackles for loss. Linebacker Kaden Elliss adds 6 pressures and 5 QB hits as a blitzer, and Pete Werner has 3 tackles for loss.

27th in EPA per dropback allowed (from 22nd), with no takeaways against Atlanta. In charting through Week 3, Kool-Aid McKinstry played every snap with 4 passes defensed and a 91 passer rating allowed on 20 targets. The touchdowns have come at safety and the other corner spot: Julian Blackmon has allowed 3 on 7 targets and Quincy Riley 2 on 15. Justin Reid has 4 missed tackles and a 114 rating allowed.

Through Week 3 (Pro Football Reference has not added the Atlanta game), coverage leaked at the back end: a 102.8 passer rating allowed (25th; league 93.2) and 8 touchdowns against 1 interception. Safeties allowed 5 of those touchdowns and a 114.7 rating while drawing 30% of the targets (league 24%). Yards per target were fine (7.0, 7th), and the linebackers held up at 87.8 on 36 targets.

Below average (19th in special teams DVOA). Daniel Carlson is 5 of 7 on field goals with a long of 51 and 10 of 11 on extra points. Ryan Wright nets 40.2 yards per punt, and Barion Brown averages 25.8 yards on kickoff returns.

New York is 3–1 with a +3 point differential, and the defense is why. It ranks 17th in EPA per play (27th a week ago) and 8th in points allowed at 19.8 per game, with eight takeaways, three of them in the 36–24 win over Arizona. The offense is 22nd in EPA per play and 26th in success rate, and scored 36 in Week 4 despite a negative EPA game (−0.09 per play).
DVOA still sees a below-average team. New York is 23rd overall, with the 29th-ranked offense and 17th-ranked defense; special teams (2nd) continue to do a lot of the work.

The Giants remain the most run-leaning offense in the league at 12.5 points below expected pass rate (32nd), with two or more backs on 34% of snaps (league 20%) and fullback Patrick Ricard on 45%. Neither look is producing: −0.09 EPA per play with two or more backs and −0.03 with one. On defense the blitz has started paying off, holding passers to −0.17 EPA per dropback with five or more rushers, while the four-man rush allows +0.12.

The Giants motion on 52% of snaps (25th; league 58%), but the offense is much better when they do: +0.04 EPA per play with motion against −0.14 without, the 8th-largest gain in the league. Passes after motion average +0.17 EPA, against −0.06 without. The defense faces motion on 55% of snaps and has handled it well (−0.03 EPA per play, 10th).

Jameis Winston has started the last two games after taking over in Week 2, and he is at −0.19 EPA per dropback (31st of 33 qualified), with completions 6.1 points below expectation and three touchdowns against three interceptions. Week 4 was his best game: 18 of 29 for 250 yards, three touchdowns and two interceptions. Jaxson Dart's 38 dropbacks are still at +0.55. The offense collapses against the blitz (−0.55 EPA per dropback vs. +0.28 without), and play action has helped (+0.24 vs. −0.04).

Cam Skattebo has 68 carries at 3.5 yards per carry, 0.5 yards below Next Gen Stats' expectation and −0.17 EPA per carry, after running right at expectation through Week 3. The blocking is the bigger problem: 1.8 yards before contact per carry (29th), and Skattebo gets more after contact (2.1) than before it (1.3). Najee Harris has added 22 carries at 4.0 yards each. Skattebo leads with four broken tackles, and the team has eight, 18th per game (Pro Football Reference charting).

Isaiah Likely is the top target with 35 (32% of the team's), 22 catches, 190 yards and two touchdowns at +0.16 EPA per target. Malik Nabers has climbed to +0.23 EPA per target (from −0.27 a week ago) with 18 catches for 208 yards. Malachi Fields is the deep option (17.4-yard depth of target, 27% of air yards) with 8 catches on 15 targets, and Darnell Mooney is at +0.54 EPA per target on 10 targets.

Andrew Thomas, Jon Runyan Jr., Francis Mauigoa and Jermaine Eluemunor have played every snap, and John Michael Schmitz and Bryan Hudson have split center. Pressure is about average (22.2%, 15th), but the sack rate has climbed to 8.7% (29th), and the line has 11 accepted penalties, four of them Runyan false starts. Runs around left end work (7.5 yards per carry), while the most-used lane, up the middle, averages 2.4 yards and −0.33 EPA.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. This now points mostly at the quarterback. Winston has turned 9 of his 22 pressures into sacks (41% vs. a 26% league rate), and FTN charged all four Arizona sacks to him, six of the team's 11 in all. The other five are split: two rushes won, two blitzes and one extended play.

Still the quietest pass rush in the league: three sacks in four games, a 2.1% sack rate (32nd), and 5.0 pressure credits per game (32nd). Abdul Carter leads with six pressures and five QB hits, Brian Burns has five pressures, and Carter and Tremaine Edmunds have a sack each. The run defense has slipped to 25th in EPA per rush.

Jevon Holland is still the playmaker, with three interceptions, four passes defensed and two forced fumbles, and Greg Newsome II has been the best corner (13 of 24 allowed, a 56.4 rating and an interception). Deonte Banks has an interception and six passes defensed but has allowed three touchdowns, as has Colton Hood (10 of 13, 138.5 rating). Linebackers Tremaine Edmunds and Arvell Reese have allowed 28 of 30, though Reese has an interception.

The coverage numbers improved sharply. New York is 8th in passer rating allowed (85.5), 4th in yards per target (6.4) and 1st in interceptions with six, although opponents still complete 63.7% (22nd). The safeties are the strength: a 47.0 rating on 31 targets with three interceptions, against a league 98.3. Cornerbacks are at 91.0 on 71 targets with six touchdowns allowed, and linebackers have allowed 30 of 33.

New York ranks 2nd in special teams DVOA. Dominic Zvada is 9 for 9 on field goals with a long of 52 and 5 for 5 on extra points. Jordan Stout has put 9 of 16 punts inside the 20 with a net average above 44 yards, and Braxton Berrios averages 27.6 yards per kickoff return.

New York is 1–3 after a 23–12 loss at Chicago, where the offense managed 157 yards and the defense gave up 495. Over four games the Jets still rank 12th in offensive EPA per play and 15th on defense, with a −8 point differential. The run game (25th) lags the passing game (12th). Ball security is the strength: one giveaway all season against four takeaways.
DVOA has dropped New York to 25th overall, from 15th. The offense fell to 19th and the defense to 19th; special teams improved from 28th to 23rd.

New York stays in one-back sets more than most (84% of snaps, league 74%) and plays slightly more tight ends than average (12th). The few two-back looks lose −0.15 EPA per play. On defense, the four-man rush has slipped to +0.11 EPA per dropback (league +0.10), while sending five or more allows +0.02.

The Jets motion less than almost anyone: 47% of snaps (30th; league 58%) and 38% of passes (31st). Plays without motion have been better (+0.07 EPA vs. −0.04), mostly because runs after motion lose −0.23 EPA. On defense, opponents' passes after motion have gained only +0.02 EPA per play (9th), against +0.17 without.

Geno Smith still leads the league in completion rate over Next Gen Stats' expectation (+10.3) and has five touchdowns with no interceptions. He ranks 14th of 33 in EPA per dropback (+0.14). It's a short game: a 7.2-yard average depth of target (24th) that lands about two yards short of the sticks. He threw only 15 passes in Chicago. Play action remains his best lever at +0.36 EPA per dropback.

The backs break tackles but don't get room. Breece Hall and Braelon Allen have five broken tackles each on runs (Pro Football Reference charting), and New York ranks 6th in broken tackles per game. But Hall averages 3.2 yards per carry, 0.2 below Next Gen Stats' expectation, and the team is 27th in yards before contact. Allen has the better success rate (45% vs. 33%), and Hall is still 10 for 10 as a receiver for 102 yards.

Garrett Wilson gets 28% of targets and 41% of air yards: 24 catches, 270 yards, two touchdowns, +0.43 EPA per target. Kenyon Sadiq's 4.9 yards of separation rank 2nd of 111 NGS-qualified receivers. Adonai Mitchell is the deep threat on a 15.8-yard average depth of target, and Isaiah Williams has 10 catches on 12 targets for 135 yards.

Olu Fashanu, Josh Myers and Joe Tippmann have played every snap and Armand Membou all but one; Dylan Parham and Jordan Meredith share the fifth spot. Pressure rate has slipped to 23% (17th, from 4th lowest), and the 8.8% sack rate ranks 30th. Run blocking is still weak at 2.0 yards before contact per carry (27th), and left tackle runs average 2.2 yards. The line has only four accepted penalties, tied for 2nd fewest.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Smith turns 39% of pressures into sacks (6th highest; league 26%), yet FTN has charged none of his 12 sacks to him. Eleven came in the pocket and seven against a standard rush, so when protection breaks, it breaks quickly.

Pressure volume has dipped to 6.8 per game (25th; league 9.3), and the sack rate ranks 15th. David Bailey, Kingsley Enagbare and Demario Davis have two sacks each, and Bailey adds three QB hits, three tackles for loss and a forced fumble. The run defense ranks 12th in EPA per rush.

The pass defense is 20th in EPA per dropback. Brandon Stephens has been the best cover man, allowing 10 catches on 22 targets with no touchdowns (64.8 rating). Azareye'h Thomas has allowed two touchdowns and a 113.0 rating, and linebacker Jamien Sherwood 163 yards on 19 targets. Opponents have made only two interception-worthy throws (league average 4.2).

The Jets allow a 92.7 passer rating in coverage (19th; league 93.2) and 6.9 yards per target (6th). Minkah Fitzpatrick's interception was the first in coverage, leaving Dallas as the only team without one. Safeties are the best group at 73.8 (8th), cornerbacks have allowed four of the five touchdowns (two each by Thomas and Jarvis Brownlee), and linebackers sit at 105.2.

Special teams rank 23rd in DVOA, up from 28th. Jason Sanders is 7 of 8 on field goals with a long of 52. Austin McNamara has punted 18 times at 48.7 yards gross and 40.1 net, six inside the 20. Isaiah Williams averages 24.1 yards per kick return.

Philadelphia is 2–2 and has been outscored by 18 after a 24–20 home loss to the Rams in which it gained 172 yards. The offense has fallen to 29th in EPA per play and 30th in success rate, scoring 18.8 points per game (26th), and the defense is 27th. The Eagles forced their first two turnovers in Week 4 but still have five giveaways to two takeaways.
DVOA is steadier than EPA. Philadelphia is 22nd overall, with the 20th-ranked offense, 22nd-ranked defense and 9th-ranked special teams.

The Eagles are still run-leaning (10.8 points below expected pass rate, 30th), mostly out of three-receiver, one-back sets: one back on 82% of snaps (league 74%), at −0.07 EPA per play. The rare two-back looks have been worse (−0.43). On defense they rush four on 78% of dropbacks and blitz only 20% of the time (league 31%), and that's the right call: the four-man rush allows +0.00 EPA per dropback (league +0.10), while five or more have allowed +0.37.

Philadelphia motions on 54% of snaps (23rd) and is much better with it: −0.03 EPA per play with motion against −0.20 without (30th). The passing game shows it most, +0.07 EPA per dropback after motion against −0.26 without. The defense is the reverse: −0.03 EPA per play allowed against motion (11th) but +0.22 without (31st).

Jalen Hurts is at −0.06 EPA per dropback (25th of 33 qualified), with seven touchdowns, three interceptions and completions 2.7 points below expectation. Week 4 was his worst passing game, 12 of 27 for 93 yards and two touchdowns, 10.9 points below expectation. He holds the ball 3.21 seconds on average (4th-longest) and is the 3rd-least aggressive thrower into tight windows. Play action has backfired again (−0.37 EPA per dropback on 26 plays).

Saquon Barkley is still the best runner here at 5.1 yards per carry and 1.1 over Next Gen Stats' expectation, but he has only 36 carries in four games and has played 38% of snaps, the same share as Will Shipley. Tank Bigsby (28 carries, 3.25 yards per carry, 0.7 below expectation) and Shipley (15 carries, 3.4) haven't come close. Philadelphia has three broken tackles in four games, 31st per game (Pro Football Reference charting).

DeVonta Smith is the volume target, with 25% of the targets and 37% of the air yards, but only +0.05 EPA per target. Dontayvion Wicks has been the bigger-play option: 197 yards on 20 targets, a 13.1-yard depth of target and 1.3 yards of YAC over expected per catch (+0.53 EPA per target). Makai Lemon has 10 catches on 15 targets for only 65 yards, while Darius Cooper and Dallas Goedert have combined for five touchdowns on 10 catches.

Jordan Mailata, Cam Jurgens and Tyler Steen have played every snap, Lane Johnson 75% with Markel Bell filling in, and Drew Kendall and Landon Dickerson have shared the other guard spot. Pressure (24.1%, 22nd) and sacks (8.7%, 28th) are both below average, and Jurgens has four of the line's 11 accepted penalties. The most-used run lane outside the middle, right tackle, averages 2.6 yards and −0.25 EPA per carry.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Week 4 shifted the picture. Hurts still turns pressure into sacks at 36% (league 26%), and FTN charged 6 of his 12 sacks to him, all in the first three weeks. None of the four Rams sacks were on him: two rushes won, one blitz and one extended play. The line now shares the blame.

The pass rush is still thin: 5.8 pressure credits per game (31st) and four sacks, a 2.6% sack rate that ranks 30th. Jalyx Hunt leads with seven pressures and four QB hits, and Nolan Smith has two sacks. The run defense ranks 29th in EPA per rush, despite four tackles for loss from Zack Baun and three from Smith.

Philadelphia is 23rd in pass defense EPA, and its first two interceptions came in Week 4, from Andrew Mukuba and Cooper DeJean. Quinyon Mitchell has held up (13 of 20, an 85.4 rating), and Zack Baun has three passes defensed. Riq Woolen has allowed 160 yards on 20 targets and DeJean two touchdowns from the slot.

Philadelphia is 16th in coverage passer rating (91.0) and has allowed only four touchdowns, 3rd fewest, but opponents complete 65.4% (25th). Linebackers are the best group at an 85.4 rating on 46 targets. Cornerbacks are at 89.0 against a league 93.3, and the safeties have allowed 11 of 14 for 216 yards, 15.4 yards per target.

Jake Elliott is 4 for 4 on field goals with a long of 58 and 9 for 9 on extra points. Braden Mann has put 10 of 19 punts inside the 20 with a 43.4-yard net. Britain Covey averages 13.5 yards per punt return.

2–2 after a 27–24 loss at Cleveland. The offense ranks 28th in EPA per play and 28th passing, though it has been positive in each of the last two games after a dismal start. The defense has slid from 12th to 14th in EPA per play and allowed positive EPA in both of those games, while the sack rate (8th) remains a strength.
DVOA has Pittsburgh 21st (−7.4%), down from 18th. The offense improved from 23rd to 18th, but the defense fell from 7th to 13th, and special teams are 24th.

Pittsburgh passes more than its situations would predict (5 points over expected, 5th highest). One-back sets, used on 80% of snaps, are still the problem at −0.23 EPA per play, while two-back looks have produced +0.32. On defense, the four-man rush (−0.06 EPA per dropback) has been far better than sending five or more (+0.36). Pittsburgh has the 3rd most linebackers on the field (4.0 on average).

Pittsburgh motions less than almost anyone (49% of snaps, 29th), and its passing game has been worse with it (−0.22 EPA per pass play vs. −0.09 without, 31st with motion). Runs are the exception: with motion, Pittsburgh averages 5.6 yards per carry against 3.1 without. The defense faces motion on 63% of plays and has handled it (−0.04 EPA per play vs. +0.06 without), especially on runs (3.6 yards per carry vs. 5.5).

Aaron Rodgers has edged up to 28th of 33 qualified quarterbacks in EPA per dropback (−0.13), with seven touchdowns and four interceptions, and completions remain below expectation (−3.0 points by NGS). Play action is still the whole story: +0.49 EPA per dropback with it and −0.31 without, the 2nd-widest gap in the league. Week 4 was his most aggressive game (27.5% of throws into tight windows), with three touchdowns and two interceptions. His receivers have eight drops, tied for 3rd most.

Jaylen Warren remains one of the league's best runners by Next Gen Stats: 5.6 yards per carry and 1.5 yards per carry over expectation, 3rd of 46 qualified backs. He has six broken tackles, four on runs and two after catches (Pro Football Reference charting), and 163 of his 309 yards have come after contact. Rico Dowdle is still at 2.5 yards per carry and a 13% success rate on 15 carries.

DK Metcalf leads with 33 targets (23%) and 38% of the air yards but has 16 catches for 213 yards, about break-even per target (−0.02 EPA), with three drops. Roman Wilson has taken on more of the downfield work (24 targets, 14.6-yard depth, two touchdowns, +0.31 EPA per target). Tight end Darnell Washington leads all 111 NGS-tracked receivers in YAC over expectation (5.5 per catch), and Pat Freiermuth has two touchdowns on 19 targets.

Zach Frazier and Mason McCormick have played every snap and Troy Fautanu all but one, while the other two spots have been split almost evenly between Spencer Anderson and Dylan Cook (49% each) and Brock Hoffman and Max Iheanachor (51% each). Pressure arrives on 24% of dropbacks (23rd), and the sack rate has climbed to 7.6% (24th). Run blocking ranks 23rd in yards before contact (2.2 per carry). The line has drawn only four accepted penalties, 2nd fewest.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Week 4 changed the picture: FTN charged all five sacks at Cleveland to Rodgers, so six of his 13 are now on the quarterback, and he turns 32.5% of pressures into sacks (10th highest of 36; league 26%). Of the rest, three came against blitzes, two on extended plays and two on a standard rush.

T.J. Watt has 4.5 sacks, eight pressures, seven QB hits, six tackles for loss and an interception. Alex Highsmith has three sacks and five tackles for loss, and Cameron Heyward has four passes defensed. Pressure volume is low (6.8 per game, 25th; league 9.3), but the sack rate ranks 8th. The run defense is 17th in EPA per rush.

Pass defense has slipped to 16th in EPA per dropback (from 9th). Patrick Queen (a 37 passer rating on 20 targets, an interception) and Jaquan Brisker (58, an interception) lead a strong second level. The corners are the leak: Asante Samuel Jr. has allowed 242 yards on 19 targets (a 133 rating), Jalen Ramsey three touchdowns, and Daylen Everette 141 yards on nine targets.

Pittsburgh holds opponents to a 58% completion rate (8th) but allows 8.6 yards per target (27th), netting an 88.9 passer rating (11th; league 93.2). Corners have allowed a 128.3 rating and all six touchdowns on 65 targets (league 93.3 for corners), while safeties (53.2) and linebackers (59.4) are far better than the league marks (98.3 and 90.8). Four interceptions in coverage rank 4th.

Chris Boswell is 7 of 10 on field goals with a long of 56. Cameron Johnston has punted 18 times, netting 42.6 yards with nine inside the 20. Kaden Wetjen averages 22.6 yards on 14 kick returns, and special teams rank 24th in DVOA. Pittsburgh has one special teams penalty, tied for fewest in the league.

A top-two defense carrying a middling offense. Seattle is 3–1 at +32, 2nd in defensive EPA per play and success rate, 3rd against the run and 4th against the pass. The offense is 13th in EPA per play: 10th through the air, 28th on the ground. Week 4's 30–23 win over the Chargers came with −0.09 offensive EPA per play, but the defense forced 4 turnovers.
DVOA has Seattle 6th (20.1%) with the No. 1 defense (−22.6%). The offense (16th) and special teams (17th) are average.

Seattle plays two or more backs on 27% of plays (league 20%) and uses play action on 35% of dropbacks, 2nd most, where it gains +0.38 EPA per dropback against +0.10 without. The defense plays the 2nd-fewest defensive linemen and 5th-most defensive backs, blitzes on 22% of dropbacks (5th lowest) and rushes four on 77%, holding offenses to −0.10 EPA per dropback when it does (league +0.10).

Seattle uses motion on 57% of plays (16th) and is worse with it: −0.08 EPA per play against +0.15 without. Runs after motion average −0.29 EPA (29th). The defense is good either way, 2nd best against motion (−0.15) and 6th without it (−0.12).

Sam Darnold has started the last two games and is 22nd of 33 qualifiers at −0.01 EPA per dropback, with 6 touchdowns, 3 interceptions and completions 6.1 points above expectation. He holds the ball 3.3 seconds per throw, 2nd longest among qualifiers. Drew Lock (+0.48, 2nd in the league, from Weeks 1–2) remains the efficiency leader. Opponents blitz Seattle on 41% of dropbacks, 2nd most, and the offense plays the same either way (+0.20 EPA per dropback against the blitz, +0.19 without).

The run game is still the weak link, 28th in EPA per carry. Emanuel Wilson averages 3.6 yards per carry (−0.37 under Next Gen Stats' expectation, 34th of 46), Jadarian Price 4.3 per carry but −0.45 EPA per carry, and George Holani 3.2. The backs get 2.5 yards before contact (15th), and Seattle has 8 broken tackles (18th per game).

Jaxon Smith-Njigba is one of the most featured receivers in the league: 37% of the targets and half the air yards, turned into 32 catches, 481 yards, 6 touchdowns and +0.77 EPA per target. Cooper Kupp has caught 9 of 12 for 114 yards and a touchdown. Rashid Shaheed (7 of 15, −0.50 EPA per target) and AJ Barner (−0.53) have been drags.

Pressure allowed is high (28% of dropbacks, 3rd most) and the sack rate has risen to 4.7% (12th) after 3 sacks against the Chargers. Charles Cross, Abraham Lucas, Grey Zabel and Jalen Sundell have played every snap while Christian Haynes, Beau Stephens and Anthony Bradford rotate at right guard. Runs up the middle (2.7 yards per carry, −0.46 EPA on 30 carries) are the run game's biggest problem.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, a measure that mostly reflects the QB) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Week 4 changed the picture: FTN charged all 3 sacks against the Chargers to Darnold. Of Seattle's 6 sacks, 3 were his fault, 2 came on extended plays and 1 when a standard rush won. Darnold is pressured on 33% of dropbacks but turns only 16% of pressures into sacks (league 26%), and Lock turned 2 of 9.

A top-three run defense (−0.23 EPA per rush) with a four-man rush that gets home: 11.5 pressures per game (6th) and 11 sacks (7.4% rate, 10th). Leonard Williams has 3 sacks, 5 tackles for loss and 6 QB hits, Derick Hall 2 sacks and 6 QB hits, and DeMarcus Lawrence 8 pressures. Drake Thomas has 4 tackles for loss, a sack and an interception.

4th against the pass, with takeaways throughout. Julian Love has 2 interceptions and a 25 passer rating allowed, and Nehemiah Pritchett (48 rating) and Josh Jobe (70) each have one. Devon Witherspoon has allowed 97 yards and no touchdowns on 23 targets.

The best coverage numbers in the league by PFR charting: a 65.8 passer rating allowed (1st; league 93.2), 5.1 yards per target (2nd) and 6 interceptions (tied for most). Opponents are 77 of 132 for 678 yards and 5 touchdowns. The safeties allow a 52.2 rating (2nd among safety groups), and linebackers see 34% of the targets (5th most; league 27%) with 2 interceptions. Ernest Jones is the most targeted defender (24 targets, 57.1 rating).

Jason Myers is 5 for 5 on field goals with a long of 57 and 12 of 13 on extra points. Michael Dickson nets 42.9 yards per punt with 8 of 18 inside the 20, and Rashid Shaheed averages 27.3 yards per kickoff return.

Still the best team in football: 4–0 with a +58 point differential, 1st in offensive EPA per play (+0.29), 1st in success rate and 1st in passing EPA, and still without a sack allowed. Week 4 was the quietest offensive game yet (+0.12 EPA per play in a 24–14 win over Denver). The defense is average (16th in EPA per play, 18th against the pass) and the run game 15th.
DVOA has San Francisco 1st at 54.8%, with the No. 1 offense (44.6%) and No. 5 defense (−13.5%). Special teams rank 22nd.

The most creative usage in the league. San Francisco has the most backs on the field (1.5 per snap, with Kyle Juszczyk at fullback) and plays with two or more backs on 34% of plays (league 20%). It also goes empty on 13% (league 6%), where it averages +1.06 EPA per play on 29 snaps. On defense, sending five or more (−0.13 EPA per dropback) has been far better than four (+0.18).

San Francisco uses motion on 80% of plays, 2nd most, and is elite either way: +0.28 EPA per play with motion (1st) and +0.33 without (2nd). Motion helps the run game (−0.03 against −0.11 without) more than the passing game. The defense is 4th best against motion (−0.08) but 28th without it (+0.16).

Brock Purdy still leads all qualifiers at +0.57 EPA per dropback, with 11 touchdowns, 1 interception and a 126.2 passer rating, and he has not been sacked on 122 dropbacks. Week 4 was his first game below expectation (completions −5.0 points), and his season figure is now +4.2. FTN has charted only 3 interception-worthy throws for the offense. Blitzing him still backfires: +1.08 EPA per dropback against the blitz.

Christian McCaffrey is efficient rather than dominant: 218 yards at 4.4 per carry, +0.26 over Next Gen Stats' expectation (11th of 46), plus 16 catches for 122 yards. He has 5 of the team's 10 broken tackles. Kaelon Black (3.9 per carry, −0.46 over expected) has been a step down, and Deebo Samuel Sr. has 74 yards on 7 carries.

Production is spread across four players. Mike Evans leads in efficiency (+1.03 EPA per target, 213 yards, 36% of the air yards) on 1.8 yards of separation; that figure includes the Week 3 lateral touchdown. George Kittle has 244 yards, 4 touchdowns and 3.2 yards after the catch above expectation. Deebo Samuel Sr. has 14 catches for 185 yards and 3 touchdowns on short throws with 4.7 yards of separation, and McCaffrey ties Kittle with 22 targets.

The best pass protection in the league: pressure on 13% of dropbacks, the lowest rate, and no sacks. Colton McKivitz and Connor Colby have played every snap, Dominick Puni and Jake Brendel nearly all of them, and Trent Williams 87%. The 3.0 yards before contact per carry ranks 3rd, but Purdy's scrambles inflate it (the backs alone average about 2.4). Runs behind right guard (−0.23 EPA on 18 carries) are the weak lane.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, a measure that mostly reflects the QB) plus FTN's charting of each sack. There's still nothing to assign: Purdy has been pressured 16 times and sacked none. The credit is shared between the line (the lowest pressure rate in the league) and Purdy getting rid of the ball.

An average rush by volume (9.5 pressures per game, 17th) that rarely finishes (3.9% sack rate, 26th; 6 sacks). Osa Odighizuwa leads with 7 pressures and 5 QB hits, Keion White has 2 sacks and 6 pressures, and Nick Bosa has 4 pressures in part-time snaps. Fred Warner has 40 tackles, 2 forced fumbles and 3 passes defensed. The run defense ranks 19th.

18th against the pass. Deommodore Lenoir has allowed 90 yards and no touchdowns on 22 targets (72 passer rating), Renardo Green has an interception and a 75 rating, and Marques Sigle has allowed 2 catches on 7 targets. Upton Stout (234 yards on 23 targets, 117 rating) and Jack Jones (2 touchdowns, 120 rating in a part-time role) are the weak spots.

Better in coverage than the EPA rank suggests. San Francisco allows an 88.9 passer rating (10th; league 93.2) and 6.2 yards per target (3rd), but opponents complete 63% (19th) and the coverage has only 1 interception (25th). Cornerbacks draw 54% of the targets (tied for 4th most; league 46%) at a 95.7 rating, while the safeties are barely tested (15% of targets, 2nd lowest) and allow a 56.4 rating.

Below average (22nd in special teams DVOA). Eddy Pineiro is 4 of 6 on field goals with a long of 57 and has missed 2 of 16 extra points. Deebo Samuel Sr. averages 25.7 yards per kickoff return, and Corliss Waitman nets 43.8 yards per punt.

An 0–4 start that is still entirely about the offense. Tampa Bay ranks 31st in offensive EPA per play, 32nd passing and 29th in success rate, and its 10.1% sack rate is the worst in the league. The defense is 6th in EPA per play and 4th against the run, which is why all four losses have been by seven points or fewer, the latest 17–14 to Green Bay with Jalon Daniels starting at quarterback. Nine giveaways against four takeaways have tipped the close games.
DVOA is far kinder than the record, ranking Tampa Bay 18th overall (from 21st). The defense has jumped to 9th (from 16th), the offense is still 24th and special teams are 14th.

The offense lives in three-receiver sets, with 2.7 wideouts per snap (3rd most) and few tight ends (30th). The defense is one of the most aggressive in the league, blitzing on 42% of dropbacks by FTN's count (3rd), and that remains its best weapon: −0.32 EPA per dropback when sending five or more, against +0.30 with four rushers. It also loads the box against the run, with eight or more on 24% of runs (league 9%).

No offense depends on motion more. Tampa Bay motions on 70% of plays (4th; league 58%) and is roughly break-even with it (−0.02 EPA per play) but collapses without it (−0.47, last in the league), the biggest motion gain anywhere at +0.45. The split is starkest on dropbacks: −0.01 EPA and 6.2 yards per play with motion, −0.60 and 2.9 yards without. On defense, the run stops are best when the offense stays still (−0.34 EPA per carry, 1st).

Baker Mayfield is last among 33 qualifiers at −0.26 EPA per dropback, with completions at expectation (Next Gen Stats), 2 touchdowns, 2 interceptions and an 80.0 passer rating, and he has been sacked on 11% of dropbacks. Jalon Daniels started Week 4 against Green Bay and went 19 of 27 for 148 yards, a touchdown and 2 interceptions (65.0 rating) on short throws (4.2-yard average intended air yards). Play action still hasn't helped (−0.39 EPA per dropback against −0.15 without), and FTN has charted 5 interception-worthy throws (8th most).

Bucky Irving is averaging 4.3 yards per carry, right at Next Gen Stats' expectation, with a 38% success rate and roughly zero EPA per carry. Tampa Bay's backs get room (2.8 yards before contact per carry, 8th), but Tampa Bay has broken only 4 tackles in four games, 28th per game, and Irving has two on 69 touches (Pro Football Reference charting). He has been a frequent but low-value receiver, 13 catches for 61 yards on 15 targets, and Kenny Gainwell has 26 yards on 13 carries.

Chris Godwin Jr. is the most efficient target, catching 16 of 18 for 142 yards and +0.33 EPA per target with 1.5 yards after the catch above expectation. Emeka Egbuka leads with 24 targets but has slipped to −0.07 EPA per target, and Cade Otton (15 catches, 157 yards) has 3 of the team's 6 FTN-charted drops (league average about 4.7). Ted Hurst III runs the deepest routes (17.8-yard average depth of target) with 1.8 yards of separation and has caught 8 of 16.

The five starters (Wirfs, Goedeke, Barton, Mauch and Bredeson) have played every snap. Pressure allowed is above average (25.5%, 27th) but not extreme, which suggests the 32nd-ranked sack rate is mostly about what happens after the pressure; see Who owns the sacks. The run blocking is better than the results: backs gain 2.8 yards before contact per carry (8th), but runs up the middle average 1.9 yards and runs behind right guard 3.1 with a 25% success rate.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, a measure that mostly reflects the QB) plus FTN's charting of each sack. It points at the quarterbacks. Mayfield turns pressure into sacks at 45% (3rd highest; league 26%), and of the 16 sacks FTN charged 5 to the quarterback and 5 more came on extended plays outside the pocket. Five came on blitzes, including two of Daniels' three against Green Bay, and only one came on a standard rush with no blitz.

A strong run defense (4th in EPA per rush) and a pass rush that depends on the blitz: 6.3 pressures per game (30th) and a 4.4% sack rate (25th). Linebacker David Walker has 2 sacks and 3 tackles for loss in 52 snaps, Josiah Trotter has an interception, a sack and 33 tackles. Alex Anzalone has struggled in coverage, allowing 15 catches on 19 targets for 212 yards and a 148 passer rating.

13th against the pass. Zyon McCollum has 4 passes defensed but has allowed a 109 passer rating, while Benjamin Morrison (78 on 17 targets) and Jacob Parrish (71 on 16, with an interception) have been steadier. Tykee Smith remains the weak spot, allowing 159 yards, 3 touchdowns and a 125 rating on 17 targets.

A 99.3 passer rating allowed (22nd; league 93.2) and 7.6 yards per target (18th), with opponents completing 65.6% of charted targets (26th). The middle of the field is still the soft spot: linebackers have allowed a 105.1 rating, mostly Anzalone, and safeties a 126.6 rating at 9.5 yards per target on 24 targets. The corners are close to league average, 92.6 on 67 targets (league 93.3).

Chase McLaughlin is 9 for 9 on field goals with a long of 59 and 7 for 7 on extra points. Kenny Gainwell (26.0) and Kameron Johnson (30.6) give Tampa Bay a strong kickoff return pair. Riley Dixon nets 36.9 yards per punt with only 3 of 17 inside the 20, the soft spot.

Tennessee is 0–4 after an 18–24 loss at Baltimore and has the second-lowest scoring offense in the league at 13.8 points per game. It is still among the most run-heavy teams, passing 11.8 points less often than expected (31st in PROE). The defense keeps games close (20.8 points allowed per game, 9th), and three of the four losses came by six points or fewer.
DVOA still has Tennessee 29th overall (−28.5%), with the 23rd-ranked offense, the 27th-ranked defense and the 30th-ranked special teams.

The Titans still play more three-receiver sets than almost anyone (2.72 receivers per snap, 2nd; league 2.43) and fewer tight ends (1.25, league 1.43). Their two-back looks have turned negative (−0.18 EPA per play on 22% of snaps, after +0.15 through Week 3). Runs against light boxes are positive (+0.09 EPA on 55% of runs), while seven-man boxes have cost −0.29 per run. On defense, sending five or more rushers keeps going badly (+0.68 EPA per dropback on 28 plays), while the four-man rush allows +0.07.

Tennessee uses presnap motion on 46% of plays, the lowest rate in the league (league 58%), and its motion plays have been poor: −0.20 EPA per play with motion (31st) against break-even without. The gap is widest on runs, at −0.19 EPA per carry with motion and +0.17 without. On defense the run defense is about break-even against motion (26th) but strong without it (−0.20 EPA per run, 6th).

Cam Ward is still playing it safe: Next Gen Stats has him throwing into tight windows on 7.6% of attempts (league 15.0%), and his average throw lands 2.7 yards short of the sticks. The result is −0.11 EPA per dropback (26th of 33 qualifiers) with completions 1.9% below expectation, 3 touchdowns and 2 interceptions; at Baltimore he went 20 of 31 for 222 yards with a touchdown and an interception. Play action hasn't helped (−0.20 EPA per dropback with it, −0.08 without).

Tony Pollard is still beating Next Gen Stats' expectation, but by less (0.21 yards per carry, 13th of 46 qualifiers, down from 0.80 after Week 3), and he is at 4.1 yards per carry and −0.08 EPA per carry on 54 carries. Tyjae Spears has added 65 yards on 15 carries. Tennessee has 4 broken tackles in four games, 1.0 per game and 28th in Pro Football Reference charting; Pollard has two.

Rookie Carnell Tate has become the clear No. 1: 32 targets (30% share), 52% of the air yards, 22 catches for 268 yards and +0.16 EPA per target, up from −0.08 after Week 3. Wan'Dale Robinson has been efficient on shorter work (16 of 23, two touchdowns, +0.19 EPA per target). Elic Ayomanor remains the big-play option with 113 yards on 5 catches, while Gunnar Helm is at −0.17 EPA per target.

Pass protection is holding up: pressure on 22% of dropbacks (10th) and a 4.4% sack rate (9th). Four linemen have played every snap, while right guard has rotated among Fernando Carmona, Atonio Mafi and Jackson Slater. Runs behind left tackle are still the problem (20 carries at 2.8 yards, −0.25 EPA each), and backs average 2.6 yards before contact (13th).

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. It still points at the quarterback more than the line. Ward converts pressure to sacks well below the league rate (21% vs. 26%), but FTN charged 3 of his 6 sacks to him and charted 2 more as extended plays. The only sack from a standard rush beating the line came at Baltimore.

The pass rush is thin as a unit: 6.8 pressures per game ranks 25th and the 6.3% sack rate is 14th. Jacob Martin leads with 7 pressures and 1.5 sacks on 57% of snaps, Jeffery Simmons has 6 pressures, 2 sacks and 5 QB hits, and John Franklin-Myers adds 5 pressures. The run defense is 18th in EPA per rush.

28th in pass defense EPA. Marcus Harris has allowed a 63.8 passer rating with an interception, and Amani Hooker has an interception but has allowed 180 yards on 17 targets. Alontae Taylor has allowed 13 catches on 15 targets for only 104 yards, and adds a sack and 4 tackles for loss.

The Titans still give up completions: opponents complete 73.4% of passes in coverage (31st), but have only 4 touchdowns (tied for 3rd fewest) on 109 targets. The passer rating allowed has risen to 102.3 (24th; league 93.2). Linebackers see 34% of targets (league 27%) and have allowed a 112.0 rating, with Anthony Hill giving up 2 touchdowns on 19 targets.

The coverage units remain the issue. Tommy Townsend has punted 21 times at 49.2 gross but 41.5 net yards. Joey Slye is 4 of 5 on field goals with a long of 42, and Chimere Dike returns both kicks (26.4 yards) and punts (7.1). DVOA ranks the unit 30th, and 8 accepted special-teams penalties are tied for 3rd most.

Washington is 1–3 and has been outscored by 34 after a 30–13 home loss to Indianapolis, allowing 30.5 points per game (30th). The offense has slipped to 21st in EPA per play and 28th in success rate. The defense has improved to 20th and has five takeaways in the last two games.
DVOA is harsh. Washington is 28th overall, with the 27th-ranked offense, 23rd-ranked defense and 26th-ranked special teams.

The offense lives in one-back sets (86% of snaps, league 74%), and those plays sit at −0.09 EPA. The defense blitzes on 47% of dropbacks, the 2nd-highest rate in the league (league 31%), and it's working better than the four-man rush: −0.03 EPA per dropback with five or more rushers vs. +0.16 with four.

Washington motions less than most teams (52% of snaps, 27th) but gets the 2nd-biggest lift in the league from it: +0.13 EPA per play with motion (6th) against −0.23 without (31st). Passes after motion average +0.25 EPA, against −0.20 without. On defense motion makes little difference (+0.02 EPA per play with it, +0.05 without).

Three quarterbacks have played. Jayden Daniels (+0.20 EPA per dropback, three touchdowns) started the first two games and Marcus Mariota (+0.09, four touchdowns, no interceptions) the last two. Athan Kaliakmanis took over early against Indianapolis and went 15 of 33 for 186 yards with a touchdown and an interception, −0.30 EPA per dropback. The offense struggles against the blitz (−0.25 EPA per dropback vs. +0.10 without).

Jacory Croskey-Merritt still has the most carries (56) but averages 2.8 yards per carry, 1.3 below Next Gen Stats' expectation (2nd-worst of 46 qualified backs), and still has no broken tackles on runs (Pro Football Reference charting). Rachaad White has been more productive: 4.5 yards per carry on 22 carries and three broken tackles on runs. The blocking isn't the main problem, at 2.9 yards before contact per carry (7th).

Stefon Diggs leads with 31 targets and has three touchdowns on 18 catches, but only 5.5 yards per target. Terry McLaurin (22 targets, 13.1-yard depth of target) has been more efficient at +0.41 EPA per target despite two drops. Antonio Williams has cooled to +0.12 EPA per target (12 catches on 19 targets), and Treylon Burks has two touchdowns on three catches. FTN charts seven drops for the team, above the league average of 4.7.

Josh Conerly and Chris Paul have played every snap and Brandon Coleman 96%, while Nick Allegretti, Matt Gulbin, Samuel Cosmi and Lucas Patrick have rotated through the interior. Pressure is still a problem (25.2% of dropbacks, 25th), but the sack rate is 3.2%, 2nd-best in the league. The right side struggles in the run game: right guard averages 1.9 yards and −0.31 EPA on 19 carries, and right tackle 2.7 yards and −0.34.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Only 5 of 39 pressures became sacks (13% vs. a 26% league rate), and FTN charged none of them to the quarterbacks: three rushes won, one blitz and one extended play. The line allows a lot of pressure, and all three quarterbacks have erased most of it.

The pass rush creates pressure, 11.3 pressure credits per game (8th), but only seven sacks (4.6%, 23rd). Odafe Oweh (eight pressures, two sacks, five QB hits) and K'Lavon Chaisson (seven pressures, 1.5 sacks, five QB hits) lead, and Daron Payne has seven pressures from the interior. Sonny Styles has a sack, an interception and a forced fumble. The run defense has slipped from 3rd to 13th in EPA per rush.

Still the weak spot, though it gave up less in Week 4. Mike Sainristil has allowed 10 of 13 for four touchdowns, and safety Jeremy Reaves three touchdowns and 155 yards on 11 targets. Amik Robertson has seven passes defensed on 30 targets (an 88.5 rating), and Rasul Douglas has held opponents to a 60.8 rating with an interception.

Washington is no longer last: a 104.6 passer rating allowed (28th, from 32nd), and it allowed no coverage touchdowns in Week 4, though its 11 for the season rank 30th. Safeties (147.3 rating, five touchdowns on 26 targets) and cornerbacks (110.2, six touchdowns) are both well above the league averages of 98.3 and 93.3. The linebackers remain the exception at 66.4 on 50 targets, with interceptions from Sonny Styles and Kain Medrano.

Washington ranks 26th in special teams DVOA. Drew Stevens is 7 of 9 on field goals with a long of 57 but has missed two of nine extra points. Tress Way has put 6 of 19 punts inside the 20 with a 41.2-yard net, and Jaylin Lane averages 24.6 yards per kickoff return.
